Our method, involving a Weighted Finite-State Transducer model, boosts recognition accuracy on targeted formats, with minimal losses in other instances. A key parameter governs the intensity of the formatting influence. The proposed technique finds applications in text analysis, particularly when dealing with formatted documents, domain-specific lexicons, or known formats like driver's license numbers and medicinal prescription terminology. We evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on a range of structured text datasets and examine its implications on overall recognition performance.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was studied in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, which outperforms baseline models in column selection and matches state-of-the-art performance in value filling.

The ongoing LoTSS survey is conducting a thorough observation of the Northern sky to better understand how the large-scale structure of the Universe changes and develops. Although only 1% of the sky is covered in the LoTSS DR1 data release, analysis shows fluctuations that need to be understood. To address these issues, mock catalogues are created to predict potential sources of error and galaxy clustering patterns in the LoTSS data are studied. The study also employs an advanced analysis technique to find the most accurate galaxy distribution and multiple object classification for the LoTSS data based on possible galaxy evolutionary stages. After eliminating areas of noisy data, LoTSS data meets the requirements for significant large-scale cosmological research. Future LoTAR data releases will provide even better data allowing more accurate measurements of the cosmos.

The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free estimation method, the HDR Lasso has been proven to provide accurate rank estimation in various applications, outperforming existing techniques. At its core, the HDR Lasso relies on a convex optimization problem, requiring two distinct penalty terms to estimate the rank of a matrix. Despite its importance, directly convexifying the penalty terms poses significant challenges, and alternative solutions involve convexifying only one term while keeping the other as a hard constraint. Building on the dual formulation, further complexities arise from quantifying the dual constraint, leading to an irregular optimization problem. By transforming this problem into a special case of a Block-Sparsity Optimization and incorporating the Exponential Weighting (EW) penalty, the HDR Lasso can be efficiently solved. Utilizing a two-stage optimization algorithm, accurate rank estimation remains Eligible for large-scale data sets.

Identifying whether an optimal solution is localized or universal is particularly challenging in complex optimization problems. This work addresses that challenge by demonstrating the existence of a single, optimal, and universal method for achieving the lowest possible rate of entropy production in fast and sluggish driving processes. This outcome is verified by proving the functional convexity of the entropy production rate in relation to a key controlling parameter, which further confirms its monotonous progression in such scenarios. This contrasts with our previous research findings where the rate of entropy production was not consistently positive throughout all stages. Our analysis demonstrates that achieving the minimum entropy production rate requires a swift and abrupt change in the controlling parameter, underscoring the importance of planarity in this regime, and also reveals how the new universal method emerges from a broader class of efficient strategies.

Over the past decade, significant advancements in artificial intelligence have positioned it as a key tool for addressing environmental concerns, primarily positive ones such as reducing greenhouse gas emissions and promoting sustainable supply chains. However, our in-depth analysis reveals that despite these benefits, AI systems are now contributing to various environmental problems, such as data-driven energy consumption and e-waste. These issues were initially overlooked due to the rapid development and high perceived utility of these technologies, but have serious long-term implications. This study seeks to uncover the root causes of these negative impacts, and explores how these harms can be mitigated through enhanced design processes that prioritize sustainability. The first step in achieving this involves creating comprehensive hazard assessments that pinpoint potential environmental harms. By examining five real-world AI-enabled technologies, our research illustrates how these assessments can identify and address AI-related environmental problems. We propose the incorporation of hazard assessments into the AI development lifecycle, and suggest design improvements to prevent or minimize these issues. The lessons from our case studies demonstrate that by incorporating sustainable design principles into AI development, the negative impacts can be significantly reduced.

This paper investigates and classifies various prescriptive process monitoring methods, which identify potential issues during business processes and provide interventions to prevent problems at the point of execution. The systematic review encompasses a comprehensive analysis of 94 studies from a database search, conducted between June 2021 and June 2022, utilizing 18 key terms. Following a rigorous examination process, the researchers extracted and analyzed data, then evaluated and classified the studies according to types of process monitoring, problems addressed, interventions proposed, methods of solution identification, and employed logic and machine learning techniques. The findings highlight the scarcity of studies on certain topics, such as intervention strategies and method annotations, indicating a potential research gap, and also point out existing limitations in current methods, including the lack of support for complex and dynamic processes, non-finite process data, and self-adaptive processes. The authors further suggest promising areas for future research in these underrepresented topics.

This study introduces an error control strategy for a Boussinesq model with adaptive coefficients, where temperature-dependent properties of heat transfer and fluid viscosity are taken into account. We primarily focus on developing indicators for the global and local errors associated with the discrete solution of the model. We derive the expression for the global error in terms of the Galerkin error, and also propose an approximation of the local error, which enables the refinement of the computational grid without solving the continuous problem. We then present methods for modifying the finite element mesh to enforce discrete continuity, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of numerical experiments involving heat transfer in porous media and natural convection in a square cavity.

Polynomial-time reduction methods, referred to as kernelization algorithms, allow large instances of a problem to be reduced down to smaller, manageable sizes within a specific time frame. These algorithms can be viewed as more complex versions of compressed sensing, where instance size is reduced via partial information extraction, and studies on their limitations and capabilities offer valuable insights into the interactions between data compression and computational complexity. This paper explores the limits of kernelization algorithms from two perspectives: how efficiently they utilize input information, and how efficiently they process sub-components. To investigate the first aspect, we develop lower bounds for specific problem parameters, such as the size of the maximum independent set, for a family of parameterized graph coloring problems. To examine the second aspect, we introduce a new class of parameterized graph coloring problems, which we use to demonstrate the intractability of certain kernelization algorithms for a wide range of related problem types, even with limited color constraints. These results leave some color selection choices unaffected and thus offer the potential for further study. To achieve these findings, we combine techniques from combinatorial theory, such as the Szemer\'edi regularity lemma and the Freiman--Grimmer theorem, with new ideas in kernelization algorithm complexity, including a novel application of the Sunflower lemma.

This study explores how opinions are shaped and social connections evolve in a complex system, governed by a delicate balance between friendly and hostile relationships. We have developed a model that captures how individuals with limited confidence in their judgments form opinions based on their personal relationships. We considered two scenarios: one where friends' opinions were reliable and another where enemies' opinions were trustworthy. To investigate the dynamic interplay between these agents, we used mean-field theory to analyze their behavior, focusing on the friends' average opinion. We found that in the first scenario, the system can either reach a stable state or experience a system collapse. In the second scenario, the system either reaches a stable state or an oscillating equilibrium. To further understand the system's behavior, we introduced external influences and conducted numerical simulations. These investigations reveal that the system can exhibit intricate, non-trivial patterns, including relative stability, complex dynamics, and around-the-clock patterns. We have presented a theoretical explanation for these observations and offered additional insights through numerical simulations.

We've investigated a newly constructed series of asymptotically flat, electrically charged black holes that form scalar "hair" when their charge increases at a fixed mass. Inside the event horizon, these black holes resemble a holographic superconducting material, exhibiting similar behavior in their scalar fields and culminating in a singularity that heavily depends on the black holes' parameters when the instability first arises. Additionally, we present a general theory in an appendix stating that certain types of stationary black holes with scalar "hair" cannot possess Cauchy horizons.

Different genes exhibiting similar activation patterns may show distinct mRNA expression levels at different time points due to variations in transcription duration, RNA degradation rates, and processing rates. The relative contributions of these factors are difficult to determine through conventional experimental approaches. We developed an advanced mathematical technique, combining system dynamics and a novel application of the Fraser-Higuchi model, to accurately predict the effects of changes in transcription duration, RNA half-life, and splicing rates on mRNA levels. This approach enables the inference of unknown kinetic parameters by leveraging the correlations among expression levels of co-regulated genes. We illustrated the technique's efficacy in simulated data and demonstrated its potential to quantify transcription duration, estimate splicing rates, and detect early alternative splicing events in real datasets from yeast and human cells.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes.

We have developed an original strategy to systematically explore and classify distinct gauge theories characterized by a specific set of anomalies, focusing on Weyl fermions and incorporating both chiral and 't Hooft anomalies in the consideration. Our methodology significantly streamlines the process of constructing and analyzing these theories, enabling the identification of all possible generalization forms of supersymmetric Yukawa theories for any given gauge group, as well as various non-supersymmetric theories that may be derived from them through mechanisms such as dualizations and conformal transformations. By applying our strategy, we are able to demonstrate that any anomaly-free gauge theory with Weyl fermions can be seamlessly transformed into a Yukawa-deformed version of its Seiberg duality partner, while also showcasing an intricate network of interconnections between these theories.

A linear complementary pair of group codes $(C, D)$ is formed when the direct sum of $C$ and $D$ results in the entire group algebra $R[G]$, given a finite principal ideal ring $R$ and a finite group $G$. We identify a required and confirming criterion for pairs of group codes $(C, D)$ in group algebra $R[G]$ to be a linear complementary pair, subsequently proving the equivalence in terms of permutations between codes $C$ and the dual code $D^{\perp}$.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our method particularly excels at handling complex probabilistic graphical models, even when the models are not inherently compact. We further developed two algorithms to optimize the size of FABE's component automata, which helps the method outperform previous state-of-the-art baselines. Our method successfully handles challenging models, such as Ising and FK-Swendsen-Wang, and even model compression yields favorable results.

The integration of multiple sensory cues, such as visual and auditory signals, is essential for pinpointing an object's location in intricate environments. Our interest lies in locating a source generating sound within a visual framework. The auditory signal is transformed into a 2D image and fed through a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN), while a region proposal network (RPN) is used to generate object regions of interest (ROI). An fully connected neural network (FCN) is applied to the object ROIs to narrow down the search space and estimate the object's vector direction. Our method demonstrates high accuracy when evaluating an auditory cue as a distinct visual channel.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework to explain viscosity spikes in terms of order parameter dynamics and fluctuations near a jamming point, and applying this theory to simulate jamming-related viscosity in two-dimensional systems, thereby supporting experimental findings that viscosity increases with order parameter to a power greater than one.

This study investigates the fluctuating electricity consumption in Ghana's period of power shortages by applying Markov switching models, namely MS-AR and AR. The data, comprising hourly electricity usage from January 1, 2014 to December 31, 2014 provided by the Ghana Grid company, helped determine the best-fitting model as MS(2)-AR(4) based on different evaluation criteria. The parameters of this model were then estimated using an expectation-maximization algorithm, indicating that the likelihood of experiencing low electricity consumption is 87%, with the low consumption period expected to last around 7.8 hours a day. The model outperformed traditional AR models by effectively modeling peak and varied electricity consumption patterns and identifying distinct regime changes during the power crisis periods.

An area where Web search personalisation may pose significant risks is in academic research, particularly in medical and scientific fields. Our investigation focuses on how Google Search responds to queries related to COVID-19 vaccination, both with and without personalised results. Our key findings reveal that personalised Search returns an estimated 80% of the relevant information it normally would, but misses essential information that could be life-altering in a public health crisis like this. To understand the extent of Web search personalisation's limitations, we examined multiple aspects, including its impact on queries from diverse professions, variations of the same query, and specific details of the vaccination process. Our analysis shows that non-personalised Google Search consistently outperforms personalised Search in returning a broader range of results, even when accounting for minor discrepancies in retrieval efficiency.

Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a task called program synthesis. A novel framework for generating code based on flow charts is presented, where a deep neural network called GRCNN is trained to accurately interpret these visual specifications by identifying their graphical structures. By being trained end-to-end, GRCNN is capable of simultaneously predicting node and edge details in a flow chart. The framework's results reveal high levels of accuracy in both node and edge prediction, suggesting its potential as a highly efficient tool for program synthesis.

This text explores multiple reduction techniques that facilitate the connection of Earth's climate models of varying complexity, emphasizing approaches that enable thorough reduction. It distills key mathematical concepts behind each method while showcasing several benchmark climate modeling examples for illustrative purposes.

The groundbreaking discovery of gravitational waves emanating from a binary neutron star merger in August 2017 paved the way for a new era in multimessenger astronomy. Kilonovae, produced by the expelled material from these events, offer scientists a crucial opportunity to explore the properties of heavy elements created via the rapid neutron capture process, or r-process. Previous research suggested that a certain type of neutron star, known as an HDEW star, emits intense X-ray and gamma-ray emissions, likely caused by the accumulation of matter on its surface. Given that these events occur infrequently, direct observational evidence of such phenomena is unlikely. A study aims to provide crucial insight into whether the reduced energy emitted from the surface of an HDEW star in the initial stages of an outburst could be responsible for its decreased X-ray and gamma-ray emission. The research employs numerical simulations to investigate the properties of an outburst on an HDEW star, taking into account varying energy flux and its effects on the surface of the star. The findings indicate that an outburst of high energy intensity would lead to a rapid increase in photon density on the surface of the star, triggering a significant decrease in X-ray and gamma-ray emission. The results also suggest that both total bolometric energy and the timing of the emission peak are influenced by the surface density of the accreted matter. The study concludes that an HDEW star in an outburst state would emit energy in the form of kilonova light, which

Radiation oncologists' goal is to target tumors accurately while shielding surrounding vital organs, specifically the stomach and intestines, from x-ray beams. The incorporation of MR-Linac systems allows real-time tumor positioning, enabling precise radiation dosage adjustments based on shifting cell populations. The manual process of identifying these organs and calibrating X-ray beams can be lengthy, extending treatment times up to one hour a day, making automated techniques with deep learning essential. A recent paper explores the use of deep learning-based automation to streamline this complex process and provide faster access to treatment for a greater number of patients.

Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This data structure is commonly found in disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. Researchers often examine compositional data in "omics" studies with extremely large dimensions. The method involves calculating logratios – the logarithmic expressions of component proportions. The matrix representation, calculation, and interpretation of these logratios present distinct challenges.

The exoplanet sample from CORALIE/HARPS (Mayor et al., 2011), which was discovered through Doppler radial velocity measurements, does not demonstrate the anticipated 'desert' at high masses (10-$100 M_\odot) with close orbital radii (<=3 AU), as predicted by the runaway gas accretion theory. Notably, similar findings have emerged from the MOA gravitational microlensing survey, which did not detect the 'desert' effect for planets in slightly longer-period orbits with lower-mass host stars (Suzuki et al., 2018). These studies collectively suggest that runaway accretion is unlikely a dominant process in shaping the final mass and orbital characteristics of exoplanets according to core accretion theory.

Artificial intelligence models, modeled after biological agents, demonstrate practical application in solving tasks that require attention and a limited scope of their surroundings.  We examine the attention and partial observability challenges in two simple tasks: a artificial agent must learn to effectively focus its attention and take in its surroundings to achieve success.  Two approaches were developed to address this issue: an inverse reinforcement learning method and a regularized policy gradient method.  We compared the effectiveness of our methods to existing solutions by testing them on a variety of environments and found that a novel inverse reinforcement learning technique outperformed existing solutions and surpassed state-of-the-art results in nearly all of the challenges examined.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and selection capabilities, mirroring brain circuit behaviors, albeit with limited applicability due to large demands. Consequently, large datasets and prolonged training times ensue. Our research introduces Locality Masked RNNs (LM-RNNs), a class of fully differentiable, fully connectable, and locally interconnected recurrent networks, capable of efficiently training on large datasets and surpassing traditional RNNs in task performance. Additionally, LM-RNNs exhibit an organic relationship between their architecture and a novel attention mechanism, facilitating the regulation of task-relevant information. Our study showcases the impressive performance of LM-RNNs on challenging datasets, such as large Language Models and the challenging MiniGame suite. LM-RNNs represent a crucial advancement in the development of efficient recurrent networks.

We categorize nilpotent algebras by dimension with a focus on their commutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties. Our findings reveal the irreducibility of corresponding geometric spaces, allowing us to accurately calculate their dimensions and establish general families of algebras associated with each space. Additionally, we demonstrate how these results contribute to an understanding of the length of anticommutative algebras in further study.

Active galactic nuclei with exceptionally powerful radio signals are among the brightest known celestial sources, spanning across a wide range of wavelengths. These powerful jets from supermassive black holes can significantly influence both the black hole's growth and its surroundings. Studies have shown that most radio-loud AGN follow a tight correlation between their black hole mass and jet power. A recent discovery of ultra-dense, millimeter-wave-emitting jets has allowed researchers to explore this correlation further. By analyzing the properties of these powerful jets in high-redshift quasars, a team of scientists investigated how radio jet power changes with redshift using data from the Submillimetre Array. They found evidence suggesting that radio jet power increases with redshift, particularly above a certain threshold of luminosity. These results suggest that as the universe aged, jet power may have evolved in a way that affects the growth of supermassive black holes and the development of their host galaxies.

We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by $c$, the speed
of light. We achieve this through the application of a suitable 'pre-non-
relativistic' geometrical parametrization, thereby facilitating an
analytical $1/c^2$ expansion of general relativity. Ultimately, this method
permits an in-depth examination of the Einstein-Hilbert action expansion up to
its next-to-next-to-leading order.

This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry by considering inversions of spatial axes and image contrast.  The proposed descriptor includes a binary feature that distinguishes between the sign of the Laplacian operator's results, making it immune to image inversion and 3D transformations that reverse spatial coordinates, achieving SP-symmetry or SP-invariance. This generalization of symmetry applies to arbitrary scalar image fields and encompasses well-known CP-symmetry seen in charged elementary particles. Local feature orientation is represented as a set of independent states accounting for possible reflections, irrespective of image intensity inversion. Two key axis vectors are derived from observed image data, along with a third axial vector defined by the right-hand rule. Adding the sign component to the traditional geometry of local features (location, scale, orientation) generates descriptors that are robust to coordinate and intensity inversions. These enhanced feature properties are integrated into symmetric kernel-based point-wise registration, modeled using binary feature correspondence. Empirical results obtained from experiments using the CPD algorithm indicate that image-based kernel-based registration exhibits increased robustness to noise and low resolution, demonstrating the efficiency of the proposed binary feature correspondence in feature alignment.

We've analyzed the light curves from the eclipsing binary system SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, and our findings suggest it's an eclipsing binary with a long period of approximately 335 days. This system likely consists of two stars of significantly different sizes, with the larger star having a radius of approximately 15 times that of the Sun, and the smaller star having a radius of approximately 1.03 times that of the He-star HD 163868. This larger star is likely a hydrogen-rich star due to its size, and the smaller star is likely a helium-rich star because of its smaller size. We estimate the temperature of the larger star to be around 9300 K, and the temperature of the smaller star to be around 8350 K. We also suspect that the larger star may be a hybrid star containing both hydrogen and helium. We've created a binary evolution flowchart to determine the possible mass range of the binary stars, and we found that the most plausible mass range for the binary stars is between 12 and 20 solar masses. We recommend further research into this binary system, including radial-velocity observations and photometric monitoring.

In numerous machine learning models and tasks, the implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. Consequently, a generalized global pooling layer for neural networks called UOT-Pooling (UOTP) has been proposed. To implement this UOTP layer, the OT problem is reformed into a differentiable optimization problem using the bregman divergence for its solution. Theoretical and experimental evaluations of UOTP are conducted, revealing its capacity to enhance the representation of images and the accuracy of classification models.

The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory. Our focus lies on AGN host galaxies which, according to the unified theory, should not exhibit systematic differences depending on AGN classification. We used the SDSS catalogue up to a redshift of 0.2, and the Galaxy Zoo Project catalogue which classifies galaxies into two broad Hubble types, and classified AGNs into two subcategories: type 1 (S1) and type 2 (S2). We compared the probability distributions of galaxy types separated by these two subcategories of AGNs, and found a significant discrepancy at the 3-sigma level, and also when considering only unobscured AGNs (at the 2.4-sigma level). These results contradict the unified theory, and may be explained by several factors, with one possibility being that type 1 AGNs reside primarily in spiral galaxies. Further investigation is required to verify these findings, and potentially restrict the established active galactic nucleus unification theory under specific conditions.

This paper delves into a comprehensive analysis of general rotational surfaces in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space, focusing on flat general rotation surfaces characterized by a 1-type Gauss map. Additionally, it's established that a non-planar, flat general rotation surface with this distinct Gauss map is a Lie group if and only if it's a Clifford torus.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by uncontrollable biases. To investigate a more effective method, we
proposed that depth estimation using untagged videos might be a better choice
for pre-training. Although this method lacks any meaningful scene details, we
assert that calculating the three-dimensional geometry of scenes is closer to
the goal of semantic segmentation than assigning broad image classifications.
Lacking an obvious benchmark, we created and implemented a new deep neural
network from scratch for estimating scene depth, which demonstrated remarkable
results when combined with subsequent refinement on smaller datasets. When
applied to driving scene segmentation, this method yielded an impressive 84.8%%
mIoU rating on the BDD-100K dataset.

The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important, but current methods have significant limitations, such as being difficult to understand and impossible to modify. We introduce TCube, a state-of-the-art time-series narration system that can visualize and accommodate new descriptions of time-series data in an easy and intuitive manner. By leveraging a cluster analysis of dimensional attributes and a timeline divided into manageable sections, TCube enables the creation of compelling, high-fidelity stories about even the most intricate time-series data, featuring detailed descriptions in an accessible format. Our case studies demonstrate that TCube significantly outperforms existing systems in both understanding and modularity. You can interact with TCube through a live demo at: https://tcube.herokuapp.com/

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

This study explores the well-posedness of global solutions, dependence on initial data, and potential loss of regularity in strictly hyperbolic equations with certain properties. These equations feature coefficients that experience moderate blow-up as sublogarithmic growth, represented by the function $|\ln t|^\gamma$ where $0 < \gamma < 1$. By applying a specific metric on the phase space, we can categorize these equations and examine their coefficients, which have polynomial bounds in x, x-derivatives, and a specific rate of decrease in t. We leverage a Planck function, based on this metric, to split the phase space and define relevant generalized symbol classes. Through the use of a conjugating pseudodifferential operator, which we term the loss operator, we establish an energy estimate and identify a link between the loss of regularity and the phase space metric and singular behavior. Our analysis shows that the solution undergoes a small, yet arbitrary, loss relative to its initial datum in a Sobolev space adapted to the loss operator.

This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. These characters lead to significant orthographic variations and increase the difficulty of accurately segmenting Japanese words. To address this complexity, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into consideration the essential global context. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed model attains exceptional accuracy when evaluated across different Japanese corpora.

On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 11,926,354 external connections to share relevant off-site information, augmenting the existing knowledge base. This collaborative effort involves repeated link sharing activities by 6,964 contributors, with over half of these interactions introducing external resources. Although these shared hyperlinks are transient, they can be captured and preserved to support knowledge base expansion and maintain consistency. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that a significant portion of these hyperlinks are relevant to existing questions on the platform, indicating a need for enhanced search capabilities to incorporate off-site information and facilitate more comprehensive knowledge retrieval.

Galactic rotation curves show a range of varying inner slopes. Observations suggest a potential relationship between a galaxy's brightness and its central dark matter, indicating the need for a more comprehensive explanation. This study investigates the potential of Self-Interacting Dark Matter, a model capable of producing compact dark matter distributions, to account for both phenomena. By analyzing a large dataset of galaxies, we find a significant correlation between a galaxy's inner structure and its dark matter interaction strength, distinct from Cold Dark Matter predictions. Moreover, we constrain strong self-interactions, limiting them to a specific threshold, and demonstrating the model's ability to explain both the diversity of galaxy profiles and the correlation between a galaxy's brightness and its central dark matter.

Although climate change is widely accepted, meaningful conversations about it are scarce,
resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we are developing a system
that leverages climate change information tailored to each person's values. To overcome initial
communication hurdles, it employs a core tenets framework, conveying the fundamental aspects
of climate change that resonate with individual values. Given the varied climate information
valued by the scientific community, our system distills this information into the selected core
tenets, ensuring the message is clear and concise. Furthermore, we are creating a user-friendly
interface to facilitate collective climate assessments, allowing anyone to contribute their perspective
regarding the current state of global climate conditions, such as temperature, sea level, and weather patterns.

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
We address this challenge by developing an adaptive framework for extracting symptoms relevant to a specific medical context.
The framework leverages a semantic network to identify similar entities and group them accordingly.
It enables context-specific adaptation by learning to recognize and group relevant entities effectively.
We evaluate our approach by testing it on three diverse clinical datasets from the BioMed NER dataset collection, focusing on three specific conditions: diabetes, kidney disease, and congestive heart failure.
Our results demonstrate an average improvement of 3.6% in F-score compared to standard deep learning models, with additional benefits of accelerated training and enhanced generalization capabilities.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive industry remains elusive. Following in the footsteps of notable achievements by Google DeepMind in mastering Atari games and Go, we have developed a comprehensive framework for autonomous driving through deep reinforcement learning. Given the intricate nature of autonomous driving, it poses a significant challenge as it necessitates tackling multiple interconnected problems simultaneously. These problems encompass sensing and mapping the environment, predicting the behavior of other road users, planning a suitable trajectory, executing a smooth and safe motion, and managing an intricate relationship between these various tasks. In order to break down this complexity, our framework divides the task into perception, planning, and execution components. These components are further interlinked through a focus on maximizing the entropy of the policy distribution to promote exploration and avoid local optima. Through collaboration between Volkswagen Group and deep reinforcement learning experts, we have successfully applied this framework to a simulated autonomous driving task and achieved a notable performance level. Our work is unique in that it is the first to apply deep reinforcement learning to a complex task such as autonomous driving. Additionally, it allows for a detailed examination of the challenges and potential of this AI paradigm in the automotive industry.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model, combining the efficiency of spiking neural networks in computation with the interpretability and flexibility of more traditional classification models. We explain the workings of this novel model, demonstrate its capacity to be a global optimum, and examine its performance in relation to alternative classification methods.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields.

Growing internet access and advancements in UDDI technologies have facilitated creation of volunteer computing platforms, allowing users to distribute computing tasks across geographically dispersed volunteers. This study proposes Pando, a novel parallel processing framework, by integrating a dynamic task division method and a volunteer management system with adaptive compensation. Pando demonstrates effectiveness through its performance in solving a real-world problem, the Traveling Salesman Problem, and exhibits potential as a viable tool for a range of applications, including data analytics, scientific simulations, and artificial intelligence, among others.

A computational method for resolving nonlinear eigenvalue problems is presented, using an approximating function derived from the eigenvalues of a modified eigenproblem equation.  By utilizing a variable sampling process that focuses data collection on the areas most critical to solution resolution, this algorithm efficiently distributes resources. It then employs the collected information to produce approximations for the sought-after eigenvalues and eigenvectors through further processing. Several numerical demonstrations highlight the performance of this solution strategy.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, thereby establishing their topological universality and exhibiting a family of conformal measures that scale non-trivially with Hausdorff dimension, definning the Hausdorff dimension itself. We also calculate the conformal dimensions of their associated systems of continued fraction expansions with a forbidden number zero.

We've found that gauge theories with $SO(N_{c})$ as a gauge group and matter fields represented as vectors confine, resulting from monopole condensation and the quark bilinear breaking $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry down to $SO(N_{F})$. Our findings derive from an ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetric theory, specifically with anomaly-mediated supersymmetry breaking.

Machine learning models such as random forests and AdaBoost have proven effective across many fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their predictions. Users are generally unable to discern how individual characteristics, or sets of characteristics, influence these models as their values change. In order to improve this understanding, a new method called Disentangled Attribution Curves has been introduced to offer more transparent explanations for tree ensemble models through detailed (multi-dimensional) sensitivity analysis results. By allowing users to visualize the models' responses to combinations of feature values, rather than just individual features, this method provides greater insight into how the models utilize their inputs. Furthermore, this approach offers a means to assess the models' dependence on user-defined subgroups. In addition to explaining model behavior, this method can also aid in identifying areas where the models may be failing, such as in the medical diagnosis domain where certain characteristics are inherently known. In contrast to other methods that focus on predicting outcomes, this method aims to promote transparency and accountability by letting users "see inside" the models. The effectiveness of Disentangled Attribution Curves will be demonstrated through its application to models analyzing patient outcomes in two real-world medical datasets.

In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on model training by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, such as using Homomorphic Encryption, can be computationally expensive or impractical at times. More recently, Trusted Execution Environments have emerged as a promising solution to enhance federated learning privacy, by safeguarding data and model parameter transmissions, yet requiring validation. In this paper, we conduct the first comprehensive evaluation of using TEEs in federated learning, by analyzing existing execution environments, assessing their capabilities in supporting secure training, and providing quantitative performance metrics, such as training speed, to aid developers in selecting the most suitable TEE for their needs. Our findings indicate that current TEEs are not fully capable of supporting secure federated learning, prompting us to suggest key improvements for future development.

The embedded systems industry is massive and ubiquitous, as evidenced by its presence in most of the world's produced processors. Interactions between drivers and external components like sensors and actuators pose significant challenges to embedded software development, particularly during the testing phase. Factors such as environmental unpredictability, limited hardware availability, and costs often hinder effective testing. To address these issues, this research presents a novel testing framework that targets driver verification on microcontrollers. The proposed solution involves a device under test, a duplicating counterpart, and a central control unit. The control unit manages testing procedures while the device under test runs the code being tested and its counterpart simulates the interactions with external peripherals. The effectiveness of the solution was confirmed through various test protocols.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can dynamically monitor system calls and make instantaneous decisions about allowed processes. In contrast to traditional static analysis-based techniques, Timeloops can function independently, run on each container, and be adapted at any moment with no predefined concepts of safe processes. Our system was thoroughly tested with a range of complex applications and demonstrated significant performance enhancements over existing methods, achieving an average improvement of 53% and a maximum of 124% when compared to the fastest alternative.

Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact, high-quality forms involve the embedding of product spaces.
We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric types, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
To tackle this problem, we first establish a framework for representing linear classification models within curved structures.
Next, we demonstrate that, regardless of the type or size of the product space, a single type of low-dimensional model can effectively represent all linear classification tasks.
This achievement marks the first time such a generalized representation has been confirmed.

This introduction focuses on stochastic Model Predictive Control methods that account for uncertainty in constraints, illustrated through a linear system under unpredictable conditions. The corresponding Matlab code is also accessible online for reference purposes.

This paper bridges the gap between compressed sensing and statistical learning, leveraging sparsity and structure to minimize the computational burden of learning tasks. We focus on independent component analysis through a compressive lens, demonstrating that certain properties within the cumulant-based ICA model yield a compact set of solutions that can be effectively represented within the cumulant tensor space. Utilizing a property known as the "identifiability through confluence," we establish that the space of compatible models is continuously connected and show that sufficient incoherence allows for the selection of a single, optimal solution. We then introduce various sampling schemes that satisfy the required incoherence conditions and propose a sublinear, convergent algorithm to estimate the optimal solution. Our results are further validated through extensive numerical experiments.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the lattice size. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration levels increase, and this shift is reflected in a parameter variation that slightly favors the long-distance species.
We prove that von Neumann algebras associated with compact regions within abelian quantum double models have infinite type $II$.

To enhance magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we develop an approach incorporating a coherent feedback loop. Furthermore, our findings confirm that both the steady and dynamic states of this system exhibit genuine tripartite entanglement. We utilize the logarithmic negativity to quantify quantum correlations between individual subsystems, as well as genuine tripartite entanglement through a nonzero minimum residual contangle. We investigate experimentally feasible parameters that enable the generation of tripartite entanglement and demonstrate its significant enhancement with coherent feedback by adjusting the beam splitter's reflective parameter. Additionally, the proposed entanglement exhibits robustness against thermal effects, making our approach a valuable asset for applications in quantum information processing.

We've obtained one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for color and spin spaces, applicable to all five scenarios: $q \to qq'\bar{q}'$, $q \to qq\bar{q}$, $q \to qgg$, $g \to gq\bar{q}$ and $g \to ggg$. The exact expressions are derived within dimensionless QCD and include the results of a specific integral up to its second-order expansion. Additionally, we've evaluated the associated splitting functions. Our results are crucial and necessary for developing subtraction and integration techniques in next-to-next-to-next-to leading order computations.

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional case algorithm, has been formulated and applied to one-dimensional local rings, and this concept is currently being used within Singular software implementation. Furthermore, a relevant theorem based on Greenberg's Strong Approximation theorem has also been introduced and applied to the realm of one-dimensional local rings.

Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore sundials through citizen science methods.

This research focuses on enhancing a D2D communication network's performance, specifically with an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) in operation. By strategically positioning IRS units within the environment, we develop an optimization problem to allocate D2D pairs in a cell and adjust the IRS parameters to maximize the network's overall spectral efficiency (SE). Due to the complexity of optimizing classical parameters (phase, amplitude, and position), we further examine the potential benefits of fine-tuning the positions of IRS units, leading to improved communication quality. To solve this non-convex optimization problem, we propose two practical solutions: an initial scheme involving a semi-spherical merit function and a more comprehensive algorithm utilizing the successively convex algorithm (SCA). We then verify the efficacy of these proposals through simulation results.

The surge in telework needs has highlighted the potential benefits of fully
automating and controlling experiments remotely. This work presents the technical
advancements of creating a two-dimensional LDV measurement system using a single-
point LDV system via a remotely controllable and automated setup. The document's
aim is to expedite the development of similar setups for this kind of application,
which is highly versatile and can be applied to various scenarios including both
air-based acoustic signal-driven samples and mechanically induced samples.

The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, which retains the same class of models but with a reduced number of variables.  The sentence $\Phi'$ uses relations of the form $xPy$ and $xQy$, where $P$ and $Q$ are symmetric properties, enabling a more structured analysis of the number of variables needed.  Our work also involves examining the spectra of first-order structures containing at least two distinct binary relations.  The combination of these results implies there is no function $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ such that for every sentence $\Phi$, the number of models containing $n$ variables and relations satisfying $\Phi$ is within the range of $f(n)$ for every fixed natural number greater than 2.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Our design employs a 
simple electrostatic lens and generates a wavefront correction over a $20 \times
10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}^2$ area with high precision. Our estimates suggest that, 
given current technology, we can attain a minimum spatial resolution of better than 
$10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$ or even reach $10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m}$ with upcoming 
 advancements in MEMS technology. Additionally, our research explores the potential 
application of ferroelectric materials, which could further simplify the design and 
manufacturing process. By achieving this, we bring closer the reality of spherically 
aberrated-free TEM imaging.

Drawing inspiration from Feynman's and Deutsch's groundbreaking work, we introduce a theoretical framework that assesses computational capability across diverse physical platforms and complexity scales. This framework is utilized to analyze the fundamental principles of quantum computation. Furthermore, this study serves as a precursor to investigating more universal computation models by examining additional physical mechanisms exemplified throughout the paper.

This study focused on determining the general equation for calculating the potential positions of an $n$ step random walk in a $d$ dimensional space with a single unit step size, denoted as $|P_n^{d}|$. Our approach began by establishing a recursive relationship for the count formula: $|P_n^{d+1}| = |P_n^d| + 2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} |P_k^d|$. We then presented two distinct methods to derive an explicit equation for $|P_n^{d}|$, involving the application of generating functions and Faulhaber's formula. Ultimately, our findings were presented in a matrix representation as our primary theorem.

This research in depth investigates the model of spherically symmetric polymer black holes, which was first introduced by Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin within the framework of loop quantum gravity. We explored how in the GOP model the spacelike transition surface at the classical singularity replaces it. Utilizing transformations in the coordinates, the authors were able to extend the metric to the white hole region, which led to discovering that the structure of the quantum black hole bears resemblance to that of wormholes, with their radii equal to each other. Moreover, the authors found that not only is the throat, but also the horizons and the spatial infinities where the energy conditions are violated. Calculations of the Ricci and Kretschmann scalars at various locations further reinforced that the throat is indeed the most quantum region of the spacetimes. Finally, the authors examined the impact of quantum effects on the quasinormal modes of massless scalar field, electromagnetic field, and axial gravitational perturbations, which was discovered to significantly deviate from their classical analogs, with all quasinormal frequencies however, exhibiting a consistent trend of decreasing as the spin parameter increases.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a novel synthesizer that addresses this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained features facilitate the expression of syntactic and logical connections. Through contextual fusion, MaskedSpeech fuses masked speech features with unmasked acoustic features. Evaluation results demonstrate that CoMA, a paragraph-level speech dataset, enhances the synthesis of syntactically related sentences in terms of mel-cepstrum, spectralvectory, and perceptual speech quality.

We've enhanced projection predictive inference by enabling efficient selection of variables and structures in models beyond linear regression. By projecting predictive variables into a lower dimensional space, we have created a generalized framework that: 1) maintains the original model's integrity while introducing no new parameters; 2) accurately detects structures and variables; 3) aspires to achieve the ideal predictive performance. Furthermore, this enhanced projection predictive inference is adaptable to various models, including generative models and neural networks. We have tested its efficacy on simulated and real-world data and have compared its performance with other variable selection methods.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, prompting the development of countermeasures against query-optimization attacks. Our research diverges from previous studies by exploring the vulnerability of DNN models to Man-in-the-Middle attacks. From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model prior to execution, whereas MitM attacks can launch without this limitation. Moreover, these attacks can only be executed internally, rendering them inaccessible via public interfaces. To overcome these constraints, we propose the first internal attack on DNN models classified as Binary Neural Networks, successfully manipulating their outputs through crafted intermediate activation layers. Additionally, to enhance the versatility of our method, we conduct a systematic analysis of possible attack vectors and outline a general framework for generating malicious inputs. Our proposed approach exhibits notable success rates in multiple datasets, highlighting its potential as a threat to BNNs.

Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly those found online. This research investigates prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing a significant Twitter dataset and applies a sophisticated stance detection technique. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations with differing levels of climate change acceptance, and reveal that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Notably, all conspiracy theories are not equally prevalent. Our findings also highlight their implications for effective climate change communication strategies.

A study focused on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been carried out using the CMS detector. This study analyzed a dataset of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of collisions. It presents the results of searches for the direct creation of dark matter along with a boson or a top quark. These results are expressed in terms of exclusion limits on the mass of the dark matter particle and its partner, assuming that they follow a specific theoretical model. This model predicts that the partner particle decays into a boson or a weak boson and a dark matter particle. This study sets the lowest masses for scalar and pseudoscalar mediator particles, based on a specific theory. It also provides the exclusion limits for vector mediator particles. This study is an extension of previous searches for similar processes.

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based angles. We also demonstrate that such a duality is always faithful. Building on previous research by Yang, we prove that in such a category, the number of duality angles n determines the dimension of the endomorphism algebra for any given object, thus generalizing his result.

Building upon Kirkeboen et al.'s (2016) work that demonstrates the feasibility of combining multiple treatment instruments with ranked preference data, we extend their analysis to include treatments with varying levels of sub-treatment categories. These categories can be considered as distinct or blended versions of existing treatments. Our primary objective is to establish under which conditions a narrow interpretation of the treatment effect is identifiable when multiple treatment instruments are applied. Notably, even with instruments that have clear cut-off points, challenges arise in determining the direction of treatment effects, and we find that these issues can sometimes be resolved using additional information from treatment combinations. The validity of our model is confirmed through applications to labor market analysis utilizing data from Norwegian survey data. The first case examines how the decision to pursue higher education affects career choices, utilizing three distinct fields of study as treatment instruments and ranking students' preferences for each field. The findings suggest a modest overall effect of attending university on preferences for any of the three fields. The second case investigates the impact of two types of job applications - part-time and full-time - which can depend on unknown numbers of sub-treatment categories. The findings indicate that applying for part-time jobs increases preferences for work-life balance but has no effect on earnings aspirations.

To advance our understanding of matter's various forms, high-energy particle collisions with a wide variety of projectiles must be studied extensively.
Although scientists have utilized beams of numerous particles to make significant breakthroughs, creating and working with beams of antineutrons, specific hyperons and their counterparts has been notoriously challenging.
However, a recent high-tech research setup known as a super $J/\psi$ factory holds the potential to greatly improve access to these elusive particles. As a result, a huge number of $J/\psi$ decays occur annually, creating favorable conditions to accurately analyze these interactions using precision-tagging of co-produced particles. 
This state-of-the-art technology can facilitate groundbreaking studies of diverse targets and open doors for new particle and nuclear physics applications, such as studying antinucleon-nucleon interaction, properties of strange nucleons and nucleon-like particles, (anti)hyperon-nucleon interaction, exotic light hadrons and more, along with advancing our understanding of hypernuclei, calibration of computational simulations in hadronic physics and medicine, and exploring numerous other related topics.

Most of a multiple star system's final mass is accumulated during the first few million years of its existence, specifically during the protostellar and protoplanetary phases.  Past research on binary systems has shown that in these systems, the majority of the acquired mass is typically added to the less massive star, resulting in statistical preferences for certain mass ratios and orbital characteristics.  Despite these findings, similar trends have not been extensively investigated for more complex star systems consisting of three or more components.  Using advanced astronomical data and observations, we examined the mass and spatial relationships of 39 hierarchical multiple star systems consisting of binaries and third bodies, and compared these patterns to those of less massive systems consisting of binaries only.  Our investigation revealed significant discrepancies in mass distribution patterns between the two sets of systems, suggesting that the way systems accumulate mass may vary depending on the level of celestial hierarchy.  Furthermore, we detected distinct differences in the spatial relationships of the components in systems consisting of binaries and triples, and these findings could impact our understanding of how these systems form and evolve over time.

This manuscript examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as viable models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale. We find that such spacetimes naturally incorporate geometric patterns suitable for describing irregular, periodically-distributed matter within the universe. We also establish mathematical proofs for their local representation, as well as the existence and uniqueness of the Einstein's equations under these specific spatial constraints. Notably, our research uncovers an interesting set of precise solutions, illustrating how these spacetimes can be used in cosmology to model a universe transitioning from homogenous, isotropic states in the early stages to more complex distributions with voids and matter peaks over time.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, which incorporates both image restoration and image segmentation components. The integration of image restoration elements addresses the issues of incomplete and imperfect boundary maps often encountered in image segmentation tasks. A specialized generator module is developed to improve the generation of complete boundary maps, and a multi-scale approach is utilized to aggregate predictive segmentation results. Experimental evaluations are conducted on both synthetic and real-world data, comparing the proposed method to state-of-the-art image segmentation models, and the results demonstrate the efficacy of our model in handling incomplete maps and outperforming conventional image segmentation models on complete maps.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear relationship between black hole mass, spin, and energy output, and applies it to a collection of 481 AGNs observed by the Large Area Telescope on the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. By establishing a limit on the maximum possible spin of observed black holes, this study explores the boundaries of observable black hole spin in low-luminosity sources.

Creating intelligent, neuroinspired systems poses a significant challenge due to its underlying hardware complexities. To overcome these challenges, a thorough comprehension of its fundamental building blocks is essential, coupled with the development of straightforward and user-friendly prototyping tools. To address this issue, an open-source emulator was designed, utilizing the Brian simulator and seamlessly integrating with existing workflows. This emulator successfully emulated error-free neural network behavior in software for individual neurons and networks of neurons connected in complex loops. Additionally, our research explored and implemented the neural network's ability to adapt through learning processes, while accounting for random numerical approximations that may affect the outcome. This project presents a unified understanding of Loihi's computational component and provides a newly designed, easy-to-use package to streamline the development of inferences and learning algorithms at the neural layer level.

A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and on very short wavelengths. The source of one such noise storm observed at 6300 MHz evolved through two distinct phases: rapid growth accompanied by rapid expansion, and gradual contraction with decreasing intensity. The source emitted two separate burst episodes during these phases, lasting around 10 minutes each, and corresponding to microflares with different energy distributions. The first burst had a more even energy distribution, with a lower energy peak of approximately 1.8 x 10^43 erg, while the second burst had a greater energy output, with an energy peak of approximately 8.3 x 10^42 erg, and a harder energy distribution. The first microflare was likely powered by the expansion of the noise storm itself, while the second microflare was likely powered by the cooling of the plasma in the storm's core.

A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating structure and a magnetic coil array on a single substrate. This novel trapping system offers improved optical and magnetic alignment stability while reducing mechanical complexity and increasing optical trapping efficiency. The integration of a broad spectrum LED and a high-efficiency optical grating achieved a saturation density of $5.1 \times 10^{9}$ cm$^{-3}$ for rubidium atoms within a $1.5\times1.5$ mm$^2$ area. This innovative MOT architecture is poised to revolutionize atomic physics experiments and sensing applications with its miniature and highly stable footprint.

The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine the case where the cloud has a finite radius. We use light-trike equations to determine the properties of the cloud. We discovered that when the cloud possesses angular momentum, its mass accretion onto the black hole is reduced compared to mass accretion in an inert cloud, which is consistent with Zeldovich's hypothesis. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the mass accretion rate is dependent on the inclination angle of the cloud's rotation axis. We have developed an expression for mass accretion that is valid for radii larger than the cloud's radius and, in the limit where the cloud's radius tends to zero, aligns with the standard, non-rotating solution.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars without bias in the less crowded regions of the galaxy.  This study examines forty candidate OB stars discovered by Mohr-Smith et al in the vicinity of Westerlund 2, with locations confirmed through spectroscopy to include seven new cluster members and thirteen confirmed non-cluster members.  The non-cluster members are primarily found in the vicinity of Westerlund 2, with distances measured to be between two and ten minutes of arc away.  It is suggested that some of these stars may have escaped from the cluster due to dynamics or ionisation, while others could have formed outside of it.  The fact that seven new members were discovered in the cluster, despite it being thought to contain only a few stars of high luminosity, supports the theory of massive star formation in less crowded environments, with a potential mechanism proposed of formation through a binary interaction within a less crowded environment that allowed for a less supersonic velocity impact.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can cause severe readability issues for current text recognition algorithms. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative, end-to-end approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks that not only restores visual clarity but also refines the linguistic content of the documents. Our novel technique differs from standard binarization methods by generating output that is both language and degradation agnostic. Furthermore, we have introduced a ground truth criterion to evaluate the effectiveness of our model in preserving the linguistic structure of the documents by assessing its similarity to the clean version of the degraded image's linguistic structure. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of our model over existing techniques in restoring both the visual and linguistic aspects of degraded document images.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian SIM card's image into its corresponding human-readable number.  This is particularly useful in an enterprise setting, where human resources may not be available to type out each customer's SIM card number manually.  While OCR has become a standard solution for this problem, it still has limitations when it comes to accuracy.  To address this, a Neuro-Linguistic Programming model was incorporated to refine the extracted text, utilizing context information to correct OCR errors.  This multi-layered approach was implemented using a Microservice Architecture, allowing for flexibility and scalability.  The results showed that the combination of OCR and NLP significantly improved the accuracy of the extraction process.

In vehicular communications using LTE, the available uplink sub-frames are limited,
leading to a difficult trade-off in allocating them to channel estimation.
Allocations excessive to pilot signals may result in unnecessary interference and
sub-frame losses, while insufficiencies can impair the accuracy of channel estimation.
