We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance measurements and quantum Monte Carlo simulations using the experimentally verified parameters confirm this analysis.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. Within the $a$SMMSM model, we investigate the connection between the axion and the dark matter generated through the anisotropic metric spinor mechanism or the hidden sector Higgs portal. Focusing on the Peccei-Quinn symmetry breaking, we find that the $a$SMMSM model generates the correct dark matter density whether the axion is overdense in the early universe or not, due to an interplay with other dark matter components.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{m+3}\log^3 m)$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$. A related algorithm subsequently uses this result to classically simulate $n$-qubit Clifford and T circuits with an improved runtime of $O((\mathrm{poly}~n) \cdot 2^{m/2 + 0.375m})$. Furthermore, the research also enhances the simulation of circuits comprising only Clifford gates, yielding a related algorithm with an improved runtime of $O((\mathrm{poly}~n) \cdot 2^{0.875m})$. All algorithmic enhancements demonstrate a significant speedup compared to the current best methods.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will reassess complex quintessence by modifying its potential and analyzing 
scalar field dynamics, followed by evaluating the differences in and stability 
of two scenarios, namely non-interacting and interacting.
We will examine the plausibility of these scenarios as real universe descriptions 
by calculating the fractional energy density, $\Omega_{D}$, and analyzing two parts 
of the quintessence field parameter space: a stiff field and a soft field.
We will conclude by highlighting the consequences of these scenarios for the age and 
size of the universe if the fractional energy density, $\Omega_{D}$, exceeds 0.8.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study, known as the LAMOST Survey of the Galactic Anti-Centre (LSGAC), which mapped approximately 4500 low-resolution spectra with a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 10, and 9000 low-resolution spectra with a signal-to-noise ratio between 5 and 10. In this research, we analyzed the results of 4500 high-signal-to-noise ratio spectra and 18,696 stellar candidates with a signal-to-noise ratio between 5 and 10. Utilizing photometry information from Gaia DR2 and DR3, we conducted a complex data analysis by implementing multi-dimensional analysis and incorporating spectral features, spatial positioning, and color space. In the signal-to-noise ratio range of 5 to 10, our analysis identified 274,658 stellar objects and 274,662 non-stellar objects. Furthermore, our team successfully cross-verified 274,658 stellar objects with Gaia DR3, reporting an overall agreement rate of 97.02% and located 273,538 new low-resolution spectra without counterparts in the Gaia catalog, accounting for 97.78% of the total LSGAC objects with a signal-to-noise ratio between 5 and 10. In the sample of LSGAC objects with a signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10, our team used the multi-dimensional method, combining radial

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures. We then devise an efficient entropy extraction circuit based on TuRaN, allowing the generation of highly random data with high throughput, low energy consumption, and reduced latency. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution achieves energy efficiency three to four orders of magnitude superior to prior work, surpasses current state-of-the-art in randomness with a throughput of hundreds of megabits per second, and is capable of generating random data continuously over an extended period of time. In addition, we provide an implementation example in 65nm CMOS technology that complies with standards, facilitating the use of the proposed solution in practical applications.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these tiny molecular constructs can process electrical signals at extremely high speeds while also storing information over extended periods and exhibiting a substantial ratio between active and inactive current levels. Additionally, simulations predict that self-organized monolayers built from these molecules could offer a practical advantage in resistive switching applications.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, providing a direct relation between loop variables and the original tree-level amplitude. This article explores all possible loop configurations in double-box processes, demonstrating that the double-box contribution to $pp\to J/\psi J$ can be fully broken down into a sum of tree-level amplitudes. To achieve this, the authors introduce a novel application of loop-tree duality, incorporating both sector decomposition and the projection strategy. To further simplify the calculation, the authors introduce the 'dual function', enabling the derivation of an analytical formula for the cross-section without direct exposure to the loop variables. This method is expected to extend to more complex processes involving triple boxes.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique in that the quantum walk's coefficients and a fundamental kernel are defined by a second-order differential equation, thereby allowing us to prove the desired eigenfunction expansion formula. In doing so, we establish the necessary boundedness of the coefficients and kernel, as well as the regularity of the quantum walk's boundaries, all while drawing connections to Sturm-Liouville theory.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Composed of two deformed cavities interacting with mechanical mirrors and coupled through a transmission parameter, this study reveals that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and magnitude of phase transitions during optical windows. Additionally, for a specified range of $q$, these systems exhibit amplification of the optical field. By manipulating parameters like tunneling strength and optomechanical coupling, one can cause optical windows to shift and vary the polarity of optical responses. This research demonstrates that $q$-deformation can tailor the optical properties of optomechanical devices.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. This led me to define R-negative states as a new class of scissors states with 1 |K| = 1; 0 components, negative charge, and classical bodies with negative space parity. Furthermore, I demonstrated that these R-negative states are associated with two-rotor systems that have a negative intrinsic angular momentum. Building on this foundation, I defined the R operator, which enables the transformation of any 0 |K| = 0; 0 state to an R-negative state, and subsequently establishes a connection between these states and negative charge states. This research paves the way for a possible link between the Two-Rotors Model's negative charge operator and the intrinsic angular momentum operator, potentially allowing for the calculation of the charge in terms of the rotor's intrinsic angular momentum.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate its electronic properties and how it interacts with the substrate. Using a computational model based on density functional theory, we found that the thin film exhibits a non-trivial electronic configuration and displays metal-like behavior, which is not typical for bulk SrVO3. Our calculations also reveal the impact of electron-phonon coupling on the electronic configuration and show that strain caused by the substrate can greatly affect the thin film's electronic properties.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In the past, scientists discovered an extension of typical behavior, designated as "anomalous" diffusion. One notable instance of this anomaly is the time-dependent diffusion process influenced by memory effects, originally studied in the context of vehicle traffic but later applied to biological systems. Furthermore, the field of anomalous diffusion is currently the focus of significant research, and we are exploring its implications in medical imaging.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly log returns linked via Granger causality. The analysis traces its development over time, focusing on years 2020 and 2021. The logarithmic US dollar price returns of this network are used for investigations. The core trading activities are found to be dominated by stable coins, which exhibit high-order statistical dependencies indicating complex price movements. The study reveals significant information dissemination among major cryptocurrencies, and further findings suggest influencable price dynamics in smaller networks. The results also show high volatility in cryptocurrency prices, particularly after receiving information from other nodes. The study validates its findings using Monte Carlo simulations and power law distributions, and further confirms the statistical significance using permutation tests.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely high supersaturated conditions needed for homogeneous water droplet formation. The application of quantum chemistry in modeling this process has improved significantly due to its enhanced precision and efficiency in calculating the configuration of particles. Nonetheless, even advanced approaches continue to rely on the classical nature of nuclei, which is uncertain for small clusters. The current research evaluates the influence of zero-point motion in the simulation of small hydronium clusters, which are formed from the trace gas acetic acid and water. The findings indicate that zero-point motion has a notable effect but does not significantly alter the particle's acidity. Consequently, it is suggested that particles with low temperatures and small sizes be modeled with a mixed quantum-classical approach, which prioritizes quantum behavior for bonded atoms and classifies the others.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions and non-expansive in nature. It's proven that every perception pair with measurements from a totally bounded space and rich enough to impose a metric on their common domain, can be isometrically embedded within a compact perception pair. Similarly, it's proven that the space of non-expansive group invariant operators can be isometrically embedded into a compact space of the same, provided the operators' images form a cover over their codomain, resulting in new compact perception pairs that compactify their original counterparts, which possess totally bounded datasets. Moreover, we devise algorithms for approximating these embeddings, which were then demonstrated using Python code to yield positive results in multiple tests.

We've investigated the impact of varying gravitational potential on sound propagation speeds and related energy transport in solid media. Utilizing a rigorous theoretical framework, we've derived non-relativistic models for long-waved phonons, taking into account both spontaneous emission and the solid's crystal structure. Our findings reveal that changes in gravitational potential can indeed influence transverse energy currents and propagate at different speeds, with potential implications for quantum experiments. Notably, we've identified a unique scenario where the energy transport is nearly lossless yet delayed, offering a potential advantage in quantum communication.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Various approaches try to tackle this task by using either traditional feature engineering or deep learning architectures, often combining both.  Despite the extensive research, it remains a complex problem to deliver universally applicable scoring systems across languages.  We present a three-component model consisting of a universal data preprocessor, a scoring network that utilizes bidirectional transformer encoding, and a layer that predicts scores and detects anomalies.  By leveraging the strengths of pre-trained transformer models like BERT and RoBERTa, we enhance the performance of conventional neural network models and achieve state-of-the-art results on two public datasets, the FEVP and TAE.  Furthermore, our system successfully generalizes when adapting to scoring essays written in a different language, demonstrated by our experiments on the FEVP-Danish dataset.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this potential in societies with social mobility limitations, we developed a model illustrating the benefits of investing in education. The model highlights two key factors: the return on investment in education for an individual with limited financial resources, and the opportunity for that investment to generate a significant return in the next generation. We analyzed these factors in the context of a large population, consisting of infinitely many individuals, with each representing a generation. Using a Markov process framework, we observed patterns in a large population, allowing us to compare the benefits of education investment for an individual with the benefits for society as a whole. The model includes variables such as the correlation between an individual's family background and their own life circumstances, as well as the positive impact of education on one's own life. Our results show that, in societies with limited social mobility, the benefits of education investment far exceed the costs, both for an individual and for society as a whole. Furthermore, we discovered that the magnitude of these benefits is particularly significant in societies with extremely limited social mobility. In contrast, we found that, in societies with substantial social mobility, the benefits of education investment are less pronounced. To examine this distinction, we introduced a new variable representing the positive impact of education on one's descendants. Our results show that, in societies with large values for this variable, the benefits of education investment are greatly increased.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
Our analysis of Delegated RingCT highlights its potential to enhance transaction processing efficiency through two primary advantages.
Firstly, Delegated RingCT enables the consolidation of multiple transactions into a single transaction, thereby increasing network throughput.
Secondly, Delegated RingCT facilitates the integration of Side Chains in XTZ, thereby enhancing Token mobility efficiency.
Consequently, Delegated RingCT poses a significant threat to the XTZ Token's dominance in the decentralized fintech industry.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's sensor equipment, utilizing a dataset totaling 137 inverse femtobarns of data.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been conducted, yielding detection confidence levels of 3.5 and 3.4 sigma for same-charge and mixed-charge scenarios respectively.  Calculated production rates of these processes, predicted using quantum chromodynamics, match observed data with reasonable accuracy.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations, validates results using automated tools, and achieves new state-of-the-art results on UD NLP tasks by combining advanced language models with innovative approaches. Additionally, the project updates and releases the existing UD HTB annotation scheme, incorporating the improvements from the new Hebrew corpus.

It is proven that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in L_p(\mu)$ where the largest absolute value among them does not exceed $K$, there exist vectors $y_1,\ldots,y_n \in \ell_p^d$ such that the following conditions are satisfied:

1. For each $i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$, $u_i$ can be chosen such that its dimension does not exceed $\varepsilon^{-2} 2^{(1/p-1/2) \cdot (1 + 2/\varepsilon)} (1 + \log_2 n)$ and its ball has a radius of $2\varepsilon K$,

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and benefits. However, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This issue restricts cooperative learning, since each new task requires retraining the network from scratch. Our study investigates two novel approaches for improving the performance of mechanics-related tasks and preventing forgetting. We developed a significant dataset with 21 benchmarks in mechanics, including input-output relationships, multi-object simulations, and complex interactive problems. Our analysis focuses on connecting machine learning with the fundamental principles of mechanics to gain insights into optimizing neural network performance. Two approaches were applied: using a gradient-mixture technique to enhance learning and a mixed-replay gradient descent method to combine skills and prevent forgetting. The results demonstrate that these methods significantly improve the performance of continual learning, especially in integrating new data. These findings promote the potential for more effective cooperative learning in the future.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research investigates LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to any degree distribution, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate our findings. Interestingly, for certain degree distribution pairs, negative degree-degree correlations yield superior results, while positive correlations can lead to better performance in certain cases. Notably, under specific conditions, degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles can surpass traditional, independently constructed LDPC ensembles even when using the optimal truncated degree distribution.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated through numerical examples.

A critical flaw exists in current quantum key distribution (QKD) implementations, which can be exploited by sophisticated attackers using advanced quantum technology. Our study proposes a novel approach that enables enhanced security in QKD by utilizing indistinguishable concurrent measurements. In this method, a quantum receptor conducts simultaneous measurements of multiple received quantum states without implementing a detection efficiency, which is a well-known vulnerability in previous QKD implementations. Our analysis demonstrates that such a mechanism provides a significant level of protection against a powerful, entangling attack. We further develop and evaluate a practical implementation of this new measurement technique. Our results show that the proposed method can effectively safeguard the key exchange process against sophisticated attacks, while also offering enhanced scalability and efficiency. Notably, the proposed measurement technique has the potential to be adapted for other quantum information processing applications.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the model's ability to learn in-context. Secondly, using a large, domain-mismatched corpus hinders the model's in-context learning capabilities. Thirdly, a pretraining corpus's size can either enhance or diminish the model's ability to learn in-context, often in tandem with its domain. Fourthly, while in-context learning may occur, it can also trigger a shift towards a more diverse range of prefix predictions, often leading to decreased accuracy. To explain these phenomena, we propose the concept of a'mental library' - an intuitive model of how a large language model's knowledge retention and recall functions.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when a cloud's core is consumed and its outer layers are displaced. To investigate this process, we created an advanced model of a 2D, colliding flow system, then simulated a cold, initially symmetric, and smoothly moving cloud of side length $L$ through a dense, stationary cluster medium. The cloud, comprising gas with initial density $\rho_0$, varied in density as it moved, while its edge crumbled under the influence of the medium's pressure, causing it to deform and develop spikes. Our 3D-like simulation revealed the following key findings: The rate at which the cloud's volume changed, as well as its surface evolution, was influenced by the ratio of its internal pressure to the surrounding medium's pressure, $p_0/\bar{p}$, and the combination of gravitational and internal forces within the cloud, $F_c/\bar{p}$. The magnitude of its internal forces was in turn determined by the combination of its internal mass and the Laplace pressure, $4\sigma/\bar{p}$, where $\sigma$ represents the surface tension within the cloud. We observed that a cold cloud that remains cohesive until it encounters the heart of the cluster can retain a distinctive shape similar to a classicaletus shape, yet its temperature disparity with the surrounding medium will increase over time. Our research suggests that some galaxy clusters possess bumpy surfaces

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as
a crucial function in validating the Standard Model's predictions and in
investigating the possible existence of new physics phenomena. The presentation
covers recent findings from the LHCb experiment, featuring measurements of
observables that Charlie Magne King refers to as "golden" and "silver," as well
as emerging areas of study.

New high-energy string interactions have been introduced in a specific theory called the NS-NS sector of open superstring theory. These interactions are called "dotted" amplitudes and have a unique characteristic marked by an odd number of dots. Mathematical expressions for scattering amplitudes of various types, including those involving two, three, four, and five particles, have been created based on a specific pattern of vertex operators and a function called the alpha function. These expressions align with previously made conjectures about a specific relationship between two types of string interactions in the NS-NS sector. A possibility of developing a new approach to string theory based on the observations made in this study is also being considered.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our joint online algorithm ensures convergence to a desired target through a stochastic approximation approach, allowing for efficient management of complex MNs. Evaluations demonstrate significant gains in reducing the cost of computation and communication compared to conventional methods.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering. The clustered units are initialized to include transient onset and decays, and steady-state rhyme components, and are subsequently rearranged into acoustic units in an HMM-GMM framework. The AU sequences are then used to develop synthesis models, and the effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through the analysis of subjective and objective scores on the Zerospeech 2019 challenge database. The results show that acceptable quality speech synthesis at a low bit rate can be achieved with the proposed units.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot.

We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states, which defy explanation through classical means. Our approach is based on two fundamental principles: the conservation of quantum resource and smooth transformations between states. We have established that efficient state transformation requires the preservation of the resource, which must not decrease in the process. Additionally, the achievable state transformation must be a naturally occurring, continuous process. By applying these principles, we were able to determine the optimal methods for measuring the quantum capacity of multi-partite states and achieving maximal quantum benefit in both bipartite and tripartite scenarios.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific assumptions, we analytically prove that DR-DSGD achieves a linear rate of convergence and has stronger theoretical guarantees compared to other robust and non-robust communication-efficient methods. Furthermore, we experimentally verify that DR-DSGD offers improved performance, particularly in distributionally uncertain settings, while also being more communication-efficient than traditional DSGD. Additionally, DR-DSGD outperforms other robust methods in scenarios with uncertain data, offering better trade-offs between communication efficiency and optimization performance.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, researchers studied how protostellar jets form and move, especially under different magnetic field conditions. Their detailed calculations considered a cloud made up of identical, rotating, and magnetized spheres that started moving and warming up, leading to the formation of protostars and outflows. These outflows turned into stable jets that traveled quickly and repeated their motion due to the strong magnetic field in the cloud. However, in simulations with a weaker magnetic field, the cloud's structure became disorganized, leading to less powerful and disconnected outflows. Jets didn't form at all in simulations that lacked a magnetic field. Their detailed results will be shared in a series of papers.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of potential threats. This assessment enables the derivation of a safety-critical constraint, which necessitates finding an optimal solution that maintains adequate performance while ensuring the system remains within its safe operational boundaries. A key challenge involves addressing the associated nonconvex optimization problem, and we propose an iterative convex optimization algorithm to achieve this. This strategy is then applied to a group of prototypical nonlinear systems as well as an actual dynamic surface control (DSC) system, and simulation results validate the efficacy of our proposed approach.

This research project seeks to offer fresh perspectives on how various gravitational interactions affect an object orbiting the Earth, specifically considering its shape and the impact of sunlight pressure. To achieve this, it provides mathematical predictions for the object's equilibrium positions, taking into account its area-to-mass ratio, initial conditions, and the object's variations in eccentricity. Estimates are also developed for the time intervals in which these orbital changes occur, which is crucial in categorizing the object's orbit under different influences. Validation of these estimates was conducted through numerical modeling and the application of specialized tools, such as the Fast Lyapunov Indicator, which helps to identify and visualize patterns related to resonance phenomena. Ultimately, this work aims to lay the groundwork for modeling the impact of sunlight pressure in the framework of established celestial mechanics models, specifically the Extended Fundamental Model.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description of optical properties, especially in the high-energy tail and non-linear responses. The advantages of the dipole gauge come at the cost of increased computational complexity, with memory demands proportional to the system size. The associated algorithm still permits the efficient treatment of large systems, allowing for a balance between accuracy and real-time numerical solving.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active shape model, where pre-defined CAD models of various objects are used as a reference, is employed to represent the shape of objects. A novel neural network approach is developed to tackle the challenge of real-world data capture and shape uncertainty. The proposed network represents both object pose and shape parameters through a probabilistic structure that uses Gaussian distributions. Consequently, optimal pose and shape estimates can be generated by minimizing a loss function, where intermediate shape predictions are iteratively refined. While traditional methods for 3D pose and shape estimation often rely on PCK (part consistency kinship) score to evaluate algorithm performance, we introduce a novel evaluation metric, PCK3. It is based on the comparison of three-dimensional point clouds and is more sensitive to shape accuracy than PCK. The proposed network outperformed existing methods in PCK3 scores on three different datasets.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size and allows information sharing between groups. We propose an approach to ensure conservative type-I error rates across all patient subgroups. Several basket trial designs are compared in terms of expected trial duration, required patient enrollment, and predicted trial completion time. The performance of our proposed approach is also evaluated through simulation studies and real-world data from a clinical trial.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems, effectively allowing for improved motion control even under dynamic conditions. The effectiveness of this innovative approach is demonstrated through simulation-based testing of a precise moving-magnet planar actuator, known to experience variations based on position during actuation and sensing.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment challenges, such as occlusions, partial overlaps, and varying scene structures. PRNet leverages PixelLink's keypoint detection capability to establish a one-to-one correspondence between points, serving as a prior to constrain and refine the registration process. To address partial credit, we propose Average Partial IPloss (APIP) and a related Partial Consistency Score (PCS) metrics. Experimental evaluations demonstrate PRNet's effectiveness and efficiency on various datasets, achieving improved results and faster computation compared to existing methods. The code and data are available for public access at the PRNet repository.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this research, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and explicitly calculate the lower central series for $\Gamma_n$. Additionally, we decompose the nilpotent quotients $\Gamma_{n,c}$ as semidirect products of finitely generated abelian groups, and we identify the nilpotent quotients $\Gamma_{n,c}$ for small values of $n$ and $c$.

Instead of presuming hypothetical new physics will be found at future colliders, 
we consider a different possibility where there isn't any. In this case, 
our main goal would be to find out if the unusual Standard Model fits within a vast landscape of possibilities. A crucial step to reach this goal would be to determine the instability scale of the Higgs potential. Achieving this requires reducing uncertainty about two key elements: the strong coupling and the mass of the top quark. Specifically, the mass of the top quark can be accurately measured by analyzing pairs of particles near their threshold at lower luminosity rates, around 10 to the 33, cm to the minus 2, per second, that might be reached with a compact e plus e minus collider using the old LEP tunnel or at a muon collider testing facility.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to expectations, we find a nearly symmetric longitudinal distribution and an obliquely shaped transverse one, indicating a substantial contribution to momentum from the strange quark.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties, primarily due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Conventional semi-supervised methods aiming to segment novel modalities typically involve extending domain-invariant representations to ensure successful adaptation. Nonetheless, simply ensuring cross-domain consistency in feature representation or prediction often falls short in transferring segmentation knowledge. To tackle this challenge, we propose an innovative segmentation task approach, dubbed knowledge distillation from domain-adapted predictions. In our method, we craft segmenter-like predictions within the source domain such that the learned representations maximize the similarity of these pseudo-labels with the target domain's annotations. Furthermore, to enhance our model's segmentation performance, we incorporate the traditional cross-domain consistency loss and entropic loss for better boundary segmentation. Our knowledge distillation from domain-adapted predictions approach demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art deep learning methods on multiple institutional multi-modal segmentation datasets.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
adversarial training, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating future
video features and anticipating actions. By using only the initial video frames and
a reduced number of parameters, Feature Mapping RNN efficiently generates future
features, which are then used in a multi-layer perceptron equipped with an RBF
kernel layer to accurately forecast actions. In our experiments, Feature Mapping RNN
achieved superior performance on JHMDB-21, UCF101-24, and UT-Interaction datasets
compared to existing state-of-the-art models.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 180-300$ nm in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction shows that the near-UV continuum flux can reach levels as high as $\approx 10^{4}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$, which suggests that the extreme ultraviolet flux in such events could potentially match or even exceed that from the host star. Furthermore, it is proposed that low-energy electrons ($\approx 10-100$ keV) are responsible for generating the hydrogen lines, generating a flare asymmetry in the $\lambda \approx 120-300$ nm band, and potentially producing faint radio emissions from gyroresonance processes. This investigation highlights the significance of combining multi-wavelength observations of superflares to gain a deeper understanding of energy release on low-mass stars.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated within the framework of spinors and Dirac operators. With this approach, we establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. Using this method, we demonstrate that instantons on Calabi-Yau 3-folds possess a natural bijective relationship with Killing vector fields, and examine the structure of the deformation space.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a specific condition under the conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be Conormal if there exists a conjugation operator $C$ such that $TC^*CT = CTC^T C$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ on the open unit disc can be described using the linear fractional form $\varphi(z) = (az + b)/(cz + d)$, where $a, b, c, d$ are complex numbers that satisfy certain constraints. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C \circ \varphi$ is C-normal when the conjugation operator $C$ is anti-symmetry with respect to the real axis. Additionally, the study explores the C-normality of Volterra type composition operators as well as tensor products of these operators.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk through a p-vertex graph, with edges assigned via the modulo p addition rule. Moreover, the research also identifies a systematic approach to accumulate the largest p-core p'-partitions of a given size, with the approach involving a recursive process on the graph's boundary vertices.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-critical domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to adversarial attacks. Our study delves into the robustness of point cloud models against transformations like rotations, translations, and scaling, uncovering unique vulnerabilities in relation to specific models and datasets. Through our research, we demonstrate that scaling presents a particularly challenging threat, causing a complete collapse in the network's latent representation. Our findings hold significant implications for the development of reliable point cloud models, prompting us to propose an algorithm enhancing the robustness of scaling within neural point cloud models. This approach involves utilizing a scale-independent point cloud synthesis technique to create transformed points. Our experiments indicate that the proposed model exhibits exceptional resilience against scaling, while also maintaining and perhaps even improving the robustness against rotational and translational transformations.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, we analyze the probabilities of interference and interference-free transmission, while introducing an innovative clear channel assessment approach for CSMA. We present and analyze a general probability formula for CSMA, considering various transmission attempts by radar units. Numerical evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of our design.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new investigation adopts a distinct approach, focusing on analyzing changes in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram resulting from entangled photon interaction. Utilizing Rhodamine B solution as the sensing medium, researchers have successfully demonstrated, through interferometric analysis, a detectable change in HOM interferogram shape indicative of non-classical phenomena. Furthermore, differences in visibility and interference fringe patterns were observed between single-photon and entangled photon-induced absorption processes. These findings substantiate the occurrence of entangled two-photon absorption in Rhodamine B solution, and the proposed method is anticipated to facilitate detection of this phenomenon in other materials as well.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a significant task to address
understanding temporal data. The task involves using incomplete temporal knowledge
graphs that detail events and their timings. A popular approach to addressing this
challenge is time-aware knowledge graph embedding, which involves representing
knowledge graph entities at different points in time. Despite efforts to
improve time-aware embeddings, existing models remain limited in their ability to
accurately predict missing knowledge graph edges. Our work addresses this deficiency
by introducing the Tanker4E model, which significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art models in
temporal knowledge graph embedding experiments. The key innovation behind our model
lies in its use of a multi-task learning framework that combines the related tasks of
time-aware knowledge graph embedding and general knowledge graph embedding. The latter
is well-established and has been successfully applied in reasoning over static
knowledge graphs. By leveraging this multi-task learning approach, our Tanker4E model
is capable of extracting rich feature representations for knowledge graph entities,
which significantly enhances its performance in predicting missing knowledge graph
edges. To validate the effectiveness of our model, we conducted thorough experiments
on three publicly available benchmarks for temporal knowledge graph embedding. The
results reveal that our model consistently surpasses current state-of-the-art models
in all evaluation metrics on these benchmarks.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from the theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in the frequency domain, based on parameters such as Poisson's ratio, damping, density, and the shape of the impacting object. Several objects with different shapes, including a flat disc, a hemispherical ball, and a cylindrical cylinder, are used in the study to calculate their natural frequencies and resonance frequencies, both in vacuum and with air present. The sound pressure spectra, normalized to the energy emitted by the objects, are also plotted for different modes of vibration, followed by a comparison of the energy emitted by the ground with that of the transient vibrations of the objects, under both impulse and impact forces. The study confirms that, in general, the sound produced by the ground is masked by the transient vibrations of the objects, but in specific situations, such as objects with low natural frequencies or those that do not have a natural frequency in the low-frequency range, the sound produced by the ground may be audible. Furthermore, the study shows that the sound produced by the ground under impact forces is significantly lower in energy compared to the sound produced by the transient vibrations,

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many researchers to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our study offers a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-perfect correlations. This research aims to clarify an enduring misconception and potentially expands our understanding of Bell nonlocality while also opening avenues for advancements in quantum information technologies.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Mott insulators transition to superconductors through flat band endorphins, harnessed in systems like triazine-based triangular lattices. We investigate the motion of dephased spin-1 bosons on a triangular lattice, applying a random magnetic field. The presence of an external magnetic field causes a transition from superconductors to Mott insulators, characterized by distinct symmetry changes in the superconducting state. We utilize the two-boson cluster approximation to analyze the system, establishing a phase diagram that maps these processes.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the form of a 2D triangular structure, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its bonds. Utilizing computational tools, we've investigated its electronic, vibrational, and thermodynamic properties. Calculations reveal that this material exhibits a unique characteristics of a B2CH2 compound, present in both bulk and single layer forms, and possesses an exceptional potential for superconductivity with a critical temperature of around 7K under theoretical pressure conditions of 10GPa.

Research on the division of quantities into equal parts continues to evolve. The findings presented here coincidentally relate to the numbers A124324 in the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences. A distinct counting method is developed for these numbers, and we establish a formula in terms of the projective representation of $S_n$. Additionally, we explore a related counting problem involving the division of quantities into the minimum number of equal parts with a specified maximum difference.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable pattern is almost entirely composed of individual, distinct patterns. Furthermore, we use this understanding to prove that certain groups are strongly stable, meaning any stable measure is concentrated on a specific, isolated part. Ultimately, we conclude that these groups are strongly stable in relation to any suitable action on a geometric space, and any stable pattern is almost entirely composed of individual, distinct patterns.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that must be impeccably functional and capable of triggering the contingency plan with precision. To ensure this, we investigate the reliability of architecture models based on formal methods, specifically using model checking to analyze potential system failures. A practical case study is demonstrated, involving a fail-operational architecture for highly automated driving systems. Model checking enables the verification of whether a system satisfies specific safety or security criteria, and this can be complemented by dynamic analysis, allowing for the identification of system failures that might be overlooked. Consequently, this can lead to adjustments in the architecture to enhance reliability and mitigate critical errors.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizing the K-Means algorithm to identify coherent patterns over varying time frames. The method's efficacy is demonstrated in simulated data and two real-world applications: identifying waves in satellite data and detecting communities in gene expression datasets.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective;  others, like Leibniz, employ an infinitesimal methodology, but its justification is disputed.  A thorough examination of the primary sources reveals that the Michael Serres' 'tense logic' scheme provides the most accurate representation of the underlying metaphysics and epistemology that supports Leibnizian calculus.  This metaphysical framework is then shown to be compatible with a number of mathematical approaches, but the traditional focus on the differential method has been misguided.

Using the effective-field-theory-based model for describing the predicted HI intensity mapping power spectrum, we investigated how its various multipoles influence the cosmological parameters' estimation. A Markov-chain-McCannay-based analysis was performed on the 220-hour data from the FastSky2 experiment and the Square Kilometre Array's expected 50-year data, both with and without noise, yielding accurate results for key parameters, including the matter density, primordial density fluctuation amplitude, and Hubble constant, with the neutrino mass and HI perturbation amplitude also constrained in the case of the SKA data.

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers n, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity. While large-scale collaborative filtering has achieved significant success, it falls short for numerous applications due to its inadequate handling of user preferences. Concurrently, deep learning has received substantial attention in the fight against data scarcity. Despite the progress made, existing methods still rely on sizable datasets, hindering their practical utility. In contrast, this paper presents a novel deep cross-modal attention network that effectively recommends items using a single user preference statement. By incorporating a preference-driven attention mechanism, our model harmoniously fuses the intrinsic and extrinsic features of the input items, yielding superior results on two benchmark datasets. Moreover, we demonstrate the robustness of our model through ablation studies on multiple aspects, including model architecture and training data. Notably, we achieved remarkable performance on the benchmark datasets, surpassing the state-of-the-art baseline by significant margins of 8.8% and 21.3% in terms of precision at 5 and precision at 10, respectively.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the asymptotic exchange property, all of these at a rate of $O(N^{-2})$. We use these properties to demonstrate the asymptotic freeness of certain bi-algebraic configurations. Moreover, this discovery paves the way for potential investigations into the asymptotic rigidity of certain non-commutative geometric structures.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and
the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$, both of which are generated by meson-meson interactions. Our analysis indicates that the primary source of isospin breaking arises from transition matrix $T$ terms exhibiting isospin breaking, followed by meson-meson mixing effects. Calculations reveal that the matrix element $T_{pp\to MP}$ related to the $p\bar p$ system is significantly smaller than $T_{d\bar d\to MD}$ matrix elements. Our findings also show that the transition probabilities for the decay reactions are notably different. More precisely, the ratio of the transition probabilities is given by $|{\cal A}_2/|{\cal A}_1|\simeq 0.42$. Our analysis further takes into account the influence of wave function contributions arising from $s\bar s$ components in $B_s$ mesons as well as the $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ resonant contributions. Ultimately, it is contingant on experimental observations to verify or refute these predictions.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a) a pupil tracker captures images of reference lasers using a $2 \times 2$ lenslet array, while b) a field tracker captures images of the science target; c) a pupil imager re-images the telescope's pupil, and d) an aberration tracker captures images of a Shack-Hartmann sensor. The camera's detector images are analyzed using dedicated software to determine beam stabilization parameters, every 0.7 seconds. The obtained parameters are then applied to a) adjust the GRAVITY instrument to align with VLTI; b) actively stabilize the telescope's pupil and field of view; c) perform defocus correction, as well as various engineering tasks. The camera has successfully transitioned into operational use, with data reduction and on-sky performance evaluations demonstrating its effectiveness.

We examine the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem, a variant of the classical k-Supplier problem, where data modification allowances are incorporated. Our study focuses on understanding the interplay between these allowances and the inherent hardness of the problem. When tolerance is limited to a specified fraction of the customer demand, we can easily obtain an efficient algorithm as a byproduct of a more general result. However, allowing a higher level of tolerance leads to a parameterized approximation scheme, whose efficiency is directly proportional to the allowed deviation. This deviation can be seen as an additional problem parameter, making the problem harder as this parameter increases. This phenomenon is similar to the occurrence in the k-Path problem in graph theory.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimal error-correcting sets of evaluations. It develops an inequality that pinpoints the minimum number of evaluations required to solve such systems with a given degree and error limit, and further proves that this inequality is often precisely met under specific conditions. Furthermore, this study identifies a particular case where the number of necessary evaluations coincides with the total number of terms across the system's polynomials, and demonstrates that, in general, the number of evaluations needed can grow in direct proportion to the system's degree and size.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic emission of photons in the cavity in sets. This phenomenon occurs when the two-level atoms are positioned in a way that inverts the electron spins simultaneously, preserving the system's parity. The emission pattern of these photon bundles is influenced by the initial state of the atoms and can be controlled to select the number of photons per unit time. We identify conditions under which the photon bundle spectrum matches the lattice frequency spectrum, allowing for the exploration of topological properties associated with it. The periodic occurrence of photons in the cavity can be utilized for generating a sequence of Fock states, which could be useful in quantum information processing.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the effects of both temperature and pressure, accurately below 10 bar, according to first-principles simulations. It enables prediction of critical points, enthalpy, entropy, heat capacity, and compressibility in a unified manner. Intercepts and slopes at zero pressure and absolute zero temperature are also included in the state equation. Evaluations at pressures up to 10 bar reveal excellent agreement with experimental and ab initio simulation data over this range.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically in the presence of malicious nodes that can deceive an estimator by furnishing fake edge information. The problem is defined as a statistical estimation issue, and we address it with an algorithm designed to withstand up to O(sqrt(n)) malicious nodes. The proposed solution, which assumes a sparse and connected network, provides accurate estimation of its size and genetic properties, specifically the number of connected components and the diameter, under certain assumptions. Furthermore, we develop an efficient algorithm for building an approximate minimum spanning tree of a malicious node-contaminated network, which achieves a constant factor approximation and tolerates up to O(n/ poly(log n)) malicious nodes.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps conventional metric perturbation solvers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the resulting degenerate system of first-order equations can be efficiently solved using iterative methods. Compared to conventional techniques, we observe a significant reduction in computational time, particularly for initial data sets involving multiple matter modes.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, the experiment's instruments require precise energy resolution and quality, which necessitated a thorough assessment of the PMTs. Over four years, a rigorous testing program for nearly 20,000 20-inch PMTs was conducted, focusing on material selection, factory testing, and on-site field testing. This extensive testing covered various parameters, including light transmission, pulse shape, and durability in harsh conditions. With over 15,000 PMTs tested, both domestic and international suppliers were evaluated, and the results helped ensure the high quality of the selected PMTs for the experiment's instruments.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent state-of-the-art LSTF methods often employ neural attention models or graph-based methods, which, although effective, suffer from high model requirements due to large parameter counts associated with attention mechanisms or graph constructions. The proposal of graph neural networks with multi-head self-attention has not been directly applied to long sequence time-series forecasting, and we fill this gap in our research.
