Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures employed thermochemical modeling using RAC2D and precise observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales project.
Our observations of C$^{18}$O J=2-1 revealed a distinct trough at 88 au that overlapped with the areas of several millimeter dust continuum emission gaps.
We observed that CO column density could be linked to dust emission, however the CO kinematics suggested itself to be a result of some sort of instability in the disk.
Our RAC2D models successfully replicated the observed column and velocity distributions and suggested that a protoplanetary disk inner disk gap could explain the substructures we saw.
Our models proposed that a massive planet with an estimated mass of around 0.02 times the mass of the Sun orbiting the star at 6.6 AU could explain the gas substructures we saw.
This planet would need to be close to 5.9 AU away from where it starts to prevent it from taking too much material away and disrupting the gas and dust emissions we see.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls, a requirement we overcome by imposing a small Lipschitz constraint on the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls, and showing that under these constraints regular paths can be closely approximated.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial alignment as expected in real, interconnected structures, contrary to earlier assumptions. Calculating the ages of these structures using the theory of molecular viscosity, we found that they are not comprised of young, co-moving stars as their names suggest. Rather, these structures are primarily composed of stars with similar distances from the galactic center, moving in the same general direction. Members of these structures show no correlation in their radial velocities, suggesting they are not physically associated. Furthermore, we found that these structures do not possess specific chemical characteristics that would indicate a shared origin. Based on these findings, we propose that these structures are not interconnected objects but rather individual stars or small groups that have become disconnected from their respective parent star clusters, or in some cases may have never been part of one to begin with.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is treated as a separate entity. Yet, in reality, a single outfit contains multiple items, whose unique attributes and style combinations contribute to an overall aesthetic. Unlike general fashion style prediction tasks, where individual items can stand alone, in search-based search-style retrieval, the entire outfit is typically considered as a single unit. To address this, our study seeks to uncover the underlying visual elements that define an outfit's aesthetic and how its components contribute to the overall look. Unlike prior research, which focuses solely on outfit photos or individual pieces, our work delves into both the outfit and its constituent parts. We introduce an new benchmark consisting of garment items and outfit pairs, along with corresponding labels. We also propose an auxiliary loss function to help the model prioritize outfit-wise visual features. Given an query outfit, our network predicts compatible items and matches, as well as identifies semantically similar outfits. Our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a significant increase in accuracy.

The framework of quantum resource theory has significantly advanced quantum physics, enabling the in-depth analysis of diverse quantum states. It plays a key role in understanding the inherent characteristics of quantum systems, aiding in the discovery of new phenomena, and guiding the precise manipulation of quantum systems. The fundamental concept of quantum resource theory involves categorizing quantum states into 'free' and 'premium' types. Operations constrained to the 'free' set preserve the resources, whereas the 'premium' set comprises states that can be converted into one another via reversible and invertible operations. We now know that these two categories can be represented by dualine projections onto a flat, directed space called a directed convex set. In this article, we delve into the general properties of such resource frameworks, investigate the conditions necessary for the existence of convex structures, and explore how the duality between free and premium sets relates to the hyperplanes of the convex structure. We also demonstrate that the 'free' set can be represented by the intersection of all cones formed by the positive, directed weights of the premium set.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators.

Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict additional dimensions with a scale separation. We've investigated a five-dimensional space with our entropy and Hawking radiation calculations, taking into account both the dark charge and gravity's influence. Our findings show that for a black hole with dark charge, the radiation rate decreases as the dark charge strength increases, and for a charged black hole, the addition of a dark photon field enhances the radiation rate. Moreover, the presence of the dark dimension amplifies the Hawking radiation.

A floating raft made of particles offers an intriguing model for observing material failure, although the factors at play are distinct from those of traditional solid materials. To investigate how particle rafts break, we developed a set-up to watch them crack while they float on a growing liquid surface. Our experiments show that, as the raft expands, a circular crack forms and spreads at a rate slower than expected, due in part to the softness of the surrounding fluid. Our findings are supported by computer simulations and can be explained using a mathematical model that takes into account both the elasticity of the particles and the fluid's viscosity.

The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In our investigation, we propose an innovative approach centered around aligning the energy levels of holes with those in silicon. This involves introducing uniaxial compressive strain along the c-axis, achieved through superlattices consisting of alternating binary and ternary layers. Our detailed calculations, taking into account a comprehensive model, reveal that matching the strain-induced energy level alignment to that of silicon accurately positions the valence band maximum. This leads to significant adjustments in mobility and mass, ultimately yielding an enhanced hole mobility of $55 \pm 5$ cm$^2$/V*s, closely matching the value for silicon. This breakthrough presents a viable pathway for developing gallium nitride-based metal-oxide-semiconductor transistors with high performance.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior distribution of the value function function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA, a new algorithm.  Our results show SPGP-SARSA outperforms traditional off-policy algorithms in both sparse and dense environments while achieving increased data efficiency.  Our approach also demonstrates a higher reward rate in underwater navigation tasks compared to the current state-of-the-art.  Our code is available for download at: \href{https://github.com/its-eth/spgp-sarsa}{its-eth.github.io/...}.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and check for continuity in that region.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We modify its domain and demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This property allows us to estimate $P$ uniformly using finite-rank operators even when $P$ isn't compact. We also establish that kernel-based techniques outperform traditional parametric methods like Galerkin methods in terms of convergence. Moreover, this research offers a new perspective on the limiting object of nonparametric estimates of $P$. Furthermore, it can be applied to other spectral analysis problems. We also provide a crucial corollary explaining the smoothness of spectral projections and nonparametric estimations of $P$.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. We explore and define the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and their associated properties. We derive recurrence relations, identities and present comparable results for $\lambda$-analogues of Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents opportunities for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this potential, previous research has not thoroughly explored the effect of temporal factors on knowledge graph embeddings. As a result, methods incorporating temporal contexts often follow a simplified approach, lacking a clear strategy to integrate temporal information. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of temporal knowledge graph projections, and specifically, a neural network-based approach, AveragePoolMultiHeadAttention, to achieve this goal. Our method was evaluated through an experiment involving the FT-GNE benchmark, and revealed superior results compared to baseline methods. Our code and data are publicly available for replication.

This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence. This line of inquiry may hold clues to understanding the nature of infinite graphs, particularly those classified as of infinite type. This note further discusses the connections between the concepts of Morita equivalence and flow equivalence within the context of higher dimensional noncommutative simplicial complexes.

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions.

To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the language model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices, thanks to the ability to infer new relationships between entities.

We have developed a novel method for constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer small vertex cover and at the same time, provide a reliable bound for their volume, making many existing examples unsuitable for practical use. Our research aims to resolve an open question posed by Panconesi and Schulman, which involves creating high dimensional expanders with efficiently small vertex cover, by applying a simple concept derived from covering spaces of graphs. Our findings provide an innovative construction method that produces high dimensional expanders with efficiently small vertex cover and a predetermined degree, thus offering an optimal solution for the problem. Additionally, we extend the Dvoretcy theorem to simplicial complexes, which gives an upper bound for their hitting sets, making our construction method nearly optimal. By applying our method, we present new examples of high dimensional expanders with efficiently small vertex cover and provide an easy-to-understand proof for Alon's theorem, which involves finding new high dimensional expanders with large spectral gap and an efficiently small expansion ratio. Our research also offers an initial approach to extending the Johnson-Lindström theorem and the Bellman-Liddo-Rosenbaum theorem to high dimensional expanders.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those not utilized during pre-training exhibit notable performance enhancements.

We have computed the Benois $\mathscr{L}$-invariants for weight one cuspforms and their corresponding adjoint representations. Furthermore, we have derived a formula that relates the image of the map from Hodge theory to the image of the Benois map, as well as provided a criterion for detecting non-diagonal $\mathscr{L}$-invariants and applications of our findings to certain Galois representations.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve these challenges, we've 
successfully integrated Rydberg atoms into a coherent spectroscopy technique, 
enabling the direct, concurrent detection of multiple frequency signals. 
Notably, our method allows for the distinction between signal amplitude and 
frequency relationships. We've demonstrated its effectiveness with frequency 
scans ranging from 50 MHz to 5.8 GHz, and have accurately measured the phase 
and amplitude characteristics of both single and multi-frequency signals. 
Given its Rydberg atom-based design, this detection method is portable and 
purchasable for even individual researchers, offering an affordable alternative 
to established methods.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a unique combination of its slow rotation rate, low surface brightness, and relatively dense gaseous disk. The exceptional star formation in this galaxy may imply the presence of a critical threshold for rotation velocity or a minimal surface brightness threshold for star formation to occur.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint.

Using the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer on board the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile Evolution/NASA Mars Science Laboratory mission, the oscillating CO$_{2}$ density in the upper Martian atmosphere, spanning between 120 and 190~km in altitude, is monitored. This observation sheds light on the effects of gravity waves (GWs), allowing scientists to analyze the behavior of GWs in the upper atmosphere under isothermal conditions and understand the role that the atmospheric background temperature plays in the propagation of GWs. Data obtained from past missions including the Mars Global Surveyor, the Mars Odyssey, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, in combination with the new MAVEN findings, reveal an association between GW-induced density disturbances and the atmospheric background speed of sound, indicating that GWs propagate more easily at higher speeds. Additionally, it becomes evident that the atmospheric density and the vertical temperature gradient have an impact on the intensity and vertical structure of GWs. While the density has a significant effect on the GWs' intensity, the temperature gradient affects their vertical structure.

The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that in the LHC's low-energy state, the proton can be viewed as comprising three components: quarks, gluons, and a photon. The latter two can interact with each another during ultra-peripheral collisions, induced by virtual photons. The simulations carried out for the p-Pb runs predicted an exceptionally large sample size of around 1 billion events, with a significant focus on single-photon and central exclusive production processes. The successful collection of data in Run 1 demonstrated the prevalence of photon-hadron interactions over expectations, with the discovery of new phenomena such as the excitation of the $\rho$ resonance and the production of $J/\psi$ particles via a mechanism not previously observed. The goals for the ongoing Run 2 and future runs include, but are not limited to: increasing precision on existing measurements; discovering new resonances; investigating the breakdown of processes into their constituent parts; and examining the patterns of these contributions; as well as examining the production of rare systems such as exclusive vector bosons, exotic states, and charmonium states.

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, low-quality sounds and using sampling-based methods. However, current models using top-notch graphics processing units can still take several minutes to sample one second of audio. Our approach presents a unified model able to produce visually relevant high-fidelity sounds and generate these in under the time it takes for audio playback on a high-end graphics processing unit. We achieve this by leveraging transformer-based acoustic models which can be trained independently, utilizing a new dataset containing full-spectrum, synthesized sound effects. This dataset combines the advantages of both automatically generated chroma vectors and human-created high-end audio assets. The integration of our model with a generated keyframe is all that's required to start sampling the sounds, resulting in improved visual relevance when compared to using randomly selected sounds.

Recurrent Neural Networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing complex sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context and the sequential transmission of information. This architecture has enabled exceptional performance in a range of significant tasks such as natural language modeling, stock market forecasting, image description, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as model predictions often depend on the specific economic scenarios being evaluated, a property known as 'economic irreversibility'. In this study, a multi-region SEIR network model is proposed with non-pharmatic interventions influencing the transmission rates and with a economic model to calculate costs based on infected populations and transmission rates. The state transition dynamics of this model determine the optimal control policy, which is found to be a computationally complex problem subject to 'economic irreversibility'. To overcome this limitation, several simplified control strategies are introduced and compared, including the basic Articulate (Ar) method, a network-informed approach, and a strategy maximizing current value. The proposed model and strategies offer insights into the critical trade-offs involved in pandemic control and economic management.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for machine learning models, which effectively measures the contribution of each training example to a model's performance, has become a prominent approach for tackling this issue. The state-of-the-art methods for calculating the Shapley value have achieved remarkable success in various applications; nonetheless, their dependence on expensive oracle calls has remained a major limitation. The advent of more advanced hardware, such as those with lower memory access constraints like Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), has further emphasized the need for more efficient algorithms. In an effort to address these challenges, we propose a novel and highly efficient algorithm for computing the Shapley value of a binary classification model on a stream of data examples. The algorithm leverages the fundamental property of additivity in probability distributions to compile the model into a concise mathematical expression, which can be efficiently analyzed one example at a time on a GPU, thus eliminating the need for oracle calls. The proposed algorithm is accompanied by theoretical proofs of its correctness, linear time complexity, and constant memory access requirements. The algorithm's practical value is demonstrated through empirical evaluations on popular datasets, which show that it significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods in terms of scalability. Additionally,

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Our experiments utilize X-ray diffraction to investigate the material's crystal structure at pressures exceeding 2.5 GPa, and find that Mn$_3$Sn maintains its hexagonal crystal structure even at high pressures. Additional experiments, including neutron diffraction and muon spin resonance measurements, confirm that the material's magnetic phase remains unchanged as it responds to pressure. The data suggests that the material's Hall effect is primarily driven by a specific type of magnetic interaction, and that the application of pressure essentially 'preconditions' the material to enter this helical magnetic ground state at zero pressure.

Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By automatically
identifying semantic relationships between entities, RE contributes to a wide range of NLP
applications, including but not limited to, knowledge graph construction, semantic
search, and deep learning model development. This paper centers on RE and provides an
in-depth review of the underlying challenges, techniques, and current research trends.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph-like data sets, where the presentation of the data is insufficient for numerous applications and a more sophisticated representation, such as a hypergraph, is required. Many of these tasks have been successfully adapted for hypergraphs, but they often come with a significant increase in computational complexity. In this study, we introduce modified measures of centrality and community detection that take into account the unique characteristics of hypergraphs, while also addressing the issue of limited data by using existing techniques to augment the representation. Our findings are then compared with those obtained through other methods using real-world data sets.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe the inner body structures. Preparing these reports necessitates medical
experts to be familiar with both normal anatomy and the detection of anomalies.
Current medical image analysis systems lack the necessary knowledge of anatomical
organization due to their narrow focus on specific tasks, such as classifyingitypes
or locations. As a result, their generated reports often contain inaccuracies and
do not adequately describe the discovered abnormalities. To rectify this issue, we
present the first unified approach to integrating anatomical information and it's
application in reporting medical images. We introduce a novel unified model that
simultaneously generates comprehensive reports by drawing from two primary sources
of information: (1) the internal structures of the human body and (2) specific
abnormalities. We also propose a new data augmentation technique for enhancing the
quality of existing annotated datasets. To assess our method's effectiveness, we
conduct experiments on two essential tasks: analogous reasoning and complete system
evaluation. Our results demonstrate that our proposed approach significantly outperforms
existing state-of-the-art techniques, yielding notable gains in both tasks.

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range and then made an educated guess that this range is the absolute minimum. Subsequent work by a different researcher, collaborating with David Gabai, found counterexamples that contradict this theory. Due to the connection between tight contact structures and taut foliations, researchers now consider the possibility that this theory could hold for tight contact structures, which are also related to Euler classes. To test this idea, recent findings show that previously found counterexamples are also related to tight contact structures, leaving room for the possibility that this theory might be correct for tight contact structures.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures.

Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, our analysis of the growing shares of negative daily returns in cryptocurrencies and their counterparts revealed a notable decline, indicating the stabilization of filtered daily returns. Finally, our investigation of the proportion of volatile days in cryptocurrencies and their counterparts showed a significant decrease, indicating the stabilization of filtered daily returns.

By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation at early time periods. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which reformulates large deviations into a nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, we reveal its complete solvability through a link with the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Employing the inverse scattering technique and a newly developed Fredholm determinant framework, we arrive at exact solutions that depend on the specific initial conditions of the KPZ equation, allowing for further generalization to other initial conditions.

The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed with data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe, researchers are able to investigate turbulent patterns down to specific frequencies. These measurements are then applied to various solar wind plasma intervals. One such interval is scrutinized, yielding valuable insights into its power spectral density fluctuations spanning from the inertial to sub-ion range. Two possible explanations for these density patterns exist, suggesting that they are a result either of specific wave types and interactions at varying scales or a broader physical phenomenon, the Hall effect. These theories are substantiated through the examination of associated electric field data.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts, with a potential for delivering over a thousand pulses per second to enable groundbreaking attosecond science applications.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
network-based approach to quantify the fairness of voting district divisions. Our
method integrates demographic information of population segments to create
candidate-preference networks, where each district corresponds to a subgraph.
By utilizing degree-based partitioning evaluation, we identified instances of
gerrymandering in synthetic data and, through collaboration with the State of
Michigan, uncovered concerns regarding candidate-preference imbalance in two of
the state's districts. While our approach currently relies on the presence of
preferential candidate information, we believe it holds promise for addressing
election manipulation and ensuring fair voting divisions in the future.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. The proposed method first detects potential regions via a two-step process, categorizing them as defects or non-defects through statistical analysis and a support vector machine. Localized regions containing defects are then further analyzed using the GHOG descriptor, which aggregates Gabor and HOG features to describe the directionality of texture, helping the binary support vector machine classify the regions accurately. The efficacy of the proposed method was demonstrated on actual fabric images with notable results.

To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the change in the environment, we improve the decision-making process. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the proposed method yields a notable increase in the navigation success rate, particularly in challenging scenarios with an elevated failure rate. The method achieves a substantial boost in the navigation success rate, reaching up to 13.2% in difficult situations, without impacting performance in straightforward tasks. The source code is freely accessible on GitHub.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7% of Population III binary remnants become located in the centres of galaxies and 5% of these merge at high redshift. If these remnants reside in the centres of galaxies for the entire duration, we predict a merger rate of one event every 100 years. However, if this is not the case, we predict a higher merger rate of one event every 29 years. Such events could potentially produce gravitational waves observable by LIGO with frequencies between 150 and 450 Hz. According to our study, LIGO should detect between one and five such events per year, or up to a total of ten such events total.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through simulations based on real-time operating data from a distribution network test bed.

Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$. The first process is predominantly driven by the $\omega$ meson. On the other hand, the cascade decays involving the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons are substantially suppressed compared to other competing diagrams, primarily stemming from the $Z$-resonance. Our findings yield branching ratios for $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ of $1.83\times 10^{-6}$ and $4.38\times 10^{-6}$, respectively.

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

The study on varying electron spin orientation employs the coordinate transformation method. Characteristically, Topological Insulators exhibit an uneven spin orientation shift within the Brillouin zone. In cases of defects, this shift occurs along closed paths in real space, with both instances characterized by non-trivial spin connections. This approach is utilized to determine the spin connections of three-dimensional Topological Insulators containing topological defects. The edge dislocation on the surface of a Topological Insulator generates a spin connection controlled by torsion, allowing electrons to move in confined circular areas and two-dimensional regions. The edge dislocations break parity symmetry, producing a current measured as a charge flux across the dislocation line.

Consider the scenario where $p$ lies between 1 and infinity, $
u$ ranges between 0.5 and infinity, and $\mathcal{S}_
u$ denotes the set of non-zero vectors in 2D space with a polar angle smaller than $ rac{\pi}{2
u}$. We introduce $R > 0$, and $\omega_p(x)$ as the p-harmonic measure of $\partial B(0,R) \cap \mathcal{S}_
u$ at point $x$ within the ball $B(0,R)$. Our findings reveal that for some constant $C$, $\omega_p(x) \leq C (1 + \log (1 +  rac{|x|}{R}))$ when the origin is the furthest point to the boundary, and that this estimate holds nearly uniformly over $x$ within some distance from the boundary of the ball. This research was motivated by its connection to the Dirichlet problem for $p$-Laplacian equations within non-smooth domains, and an extension of this was also explored to higher dimensions.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2013. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers.

Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-dependent information, significantly contributing to teaching robots human-like motion through emulation. In robotics literature, this concept has gained considerable attention. Despite its importance, there has been a significant lack of relevant spatial data sources available for public use. In order to bridge this gap, we developed an system to automatically generate manipulability ellipsoids from any 3D pose data set. Our method can be applied to any human-like agent, such as humans and robots, and provides a useful tool for a wide range of applications in robotics and computer graphics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our system by using it to create manipulability ellipsoids from the CMU Panorama, Surreal, and Human3.6M data sets.

To explore non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\text{HH} \to \text{b}\bar{\text{b}}\text{W}\text{W}^*$ channel, we investigate the feasibility of reconstructing the Higgs boson pairs using deep neural networks. By leveraging the LHC's proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV and with a combined 120 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ luminosity, we generate around 19,000 signal events and 3.6 $\times$ 10$^{6}$ background occurrences. Applying the AI-based algorithm to both signal and background situations, we compute an overall efficiency of 0.044% for a fake-free region. Under the assumption of no new physics influence, we establish a 95% confidence level upper limit of 3.1 $\text{pb}$. Additionally, we find that beyond the standard model effects can lead to a modulation in the predicted cross-section, amounting to a 25% change.

A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video data. Distinguishing it from existing approaches, this method leverages video frames without an initial coarse pose, thereby allowing any view to be predicted. Unlike pose-based datasets, these video frames offer diverse contextual clues that can enhance learning, particularly for objects with irregular shapes. A two-stage process is employed, initially using a deep network to pair views and then refining the results through joint optimization. Notably, this method achieves comparable performance to leading domain-specific methods while demonstrating improved robustness on objects with irregular shapes.

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can discern one's attitude toward this misinformation. This new framework leverages neural networks and attitude consistency to classify stances toward COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. A novel neural framework, called AttMISNet, has been devised to differentiate between misinformation believers and skeptics, expressing their skepticism or confirmation through comments on social media platforms. Experiments were conducted on a newly created dataset, consisting of Twitter data, which reveals that AttMISNet achieves impressive performance with high accuracy rates.

Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to unveil the core electronic behavior of matter, contingent on achieving two interconnected technological milestones linked to high-order harmonic generation sources. Firstly, achieving a higher photon flux would allow researchers to measure even the faintest electronic processes, while also attaining better spectral tunability would grant selectivity in targeting specific electronic transitions. Breakthroughs are made feasible by parametric waveform synthesis, giving scientists the capability to craft controllable, highly-tunable high-energy electric transients. We illustrate the practical implementation of this innovation in two experiments, demonstrating the capability to produce few-cycle, tunable attosecond pulses via nonlinear interaction with rare-gas atoms. We have successfully produced pulses with energies of hundreds of eV, alongside a tunable XUV pulse, yielding a notable intersection point at 42 eV, offering a pathway to attosecond science enhanced by parametric waveform synthesis.

Eclipse predictions for binary stars can be significantly improved by revising older data, which we have done for Algol (alfegma, algedi) using modern time-scale values. This update takes into account recent research on radio pulsars and binary systems from the field of pulsar timing. Accurate data on Algol's eclipses revealed periodic fluctuations in its observed epoch times, which can be explained by changes in its light-scattering particles. This phenomenon occurs due to the varying temperatures of these particles, which depend on the binary's changing separation and take about 33 years to fully adjust. This unique situation in Algol provides valuable insight into the effects of dust particles on our understanding of eclipsing binary systems.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A key aspect of our analysis involves deriving a new, improved version of the Strichartz estimate for this problem.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency are required for this approach. To address this need, enhancing training point generation is an important direction of investigation. Both adaptive and quasi-uniform sampling techniques have previously been explored, each showing benefits. To leverage these insights, we introduce Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, which combines an adjustable nodal distribution method and a memory mechanism. We then conduct experiments on both linear and nonlinear PDEs, evaluating its accuracy and efficiency relative to traditional sampling methods.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the oscillations in their electrostatic conduction band profile, which are characteristic of these devices. We model these dynamics by solving coupled two-dimensional Poisson's equations and energy equations, and find that the system converges to a stable thermodynamic state through energy minimization. We also investigate how the device responds to various input voltages and the time it takes for these domains to form or change (called switching times), which are significant parameters in the device's performance.

A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the security of open-source libraries within Cargo, as existing research focused on C and C++ is limited to Linux and Unix systems. Our investigation, the first of its kind in the Rust community, involves multiple contributors and stakeholders. We developed a unique methodology to collect and analyze crate graphs, and established the Cargo Security Database, containing vulnerability data not previously available. Our analysis reveals that Cargo ecosystem vulnerabilities primarily stem from memory-related issues, and semantic versioning inconsistencies pose a challenge for vulnerability tracking. Furthermore, we discovered a lack of security best practices among developers, and identified education as a key improvement area. Our study sheds light on the existing security issues in the Rust community, and potentially harms end-users. We hope our research and findings will inspire further investigation and contribute to enhancing software library security.

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to demonstrate irreducibility. This paper confirms the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subjected to discrete jump noises and shows these results apply universally across all initial conditions. A key factor in this proof involves establishing a majorized condition to describe how jump noises interact within the system.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing its power graph, specifically the minimal vertex degree. This power graph connects vertices based on one being a power of another, and its edges represent elements that are powers of each other. By examining the group's prime divisors and Sylow subgroups, we've established a connection between the minimal degree and these subgroups. Additionally, we've studied the degree in specific types of groups: dihedrals and SDels.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively studied at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 GeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the characteristics of cosmic ray showers.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing a matrix factorization framework with sparsity and low-rank constraints to integrate local and global structures. Through the propagation of this low-rank structure, our method achieves significantly improved sparsity for representing the original Gabor filter bank. Our experimental results show that OCNs outperform existing DCNN-based methods, specifically for applications like face recognition and handwritten digit classification.

This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency and adaptability of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) suited for point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's spatial structure can be fully exploited by the KNN search, eliminating the need for additional spatial encoding. Secondly, the learned parameters within the multilayer perceptron possess inherent redundancy, prompting us to introduce a sub-network pruning approach based on the Frobenius norm of matrix decomposition. Through extensive experiments, our proposed efficient GCN demonstrates superior computational efficiency while maintaining or even surpassing the accuracy of baseline GCN implementations.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing Trojan attacks, which embed inconsequential triggers in clean images, our method considers trigger images as full-resolution representations of meaningful object categories. As our backdoored classifier is designed to recognize the inherent concepts of trigger images rather than specific patterns, it can be triggered by semantically similar images with distinct appearances, making our attack more applicable and resilient to countermeasures in real-world scenarios. Our experiments show that even with limited Trojan patterns, our approach can adapt to new trigger images within the same category and evade sophisticated defense strategies effectively.

We are developing an image slicer for an integral field unit, ROSIE IFU, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. By splitting the 50.4 x 53.5 field of view into four subfields, and further segmenting these into 21 individual 0.6 x 53.5 slices, we'll achieve four pseudo-slits, spaced six arcminutes apart. This will allow for a spectral range of 1800 Angstroms with a resolution of 2000. Our current progress includes crafting the slicer's metal structure, coating the internal surfaces, and assembling the optics. Once completed, ROSIE IFU will enable the simultaneous study of large areas, facilitating the discovery of faint, rapidly moving objects, like Kuiper belt objects and exoplanets, by providing a wide-field view of their movements.

In astrophysical contexts, carbon-carbon fusion is significant for both natural events, such as novae, supernovae, and red giant stars, and human-created experiments like the Large Hadron Collider. The experiments aimed to verify the CC fusion at the low energy level of 64 MeV, but surprisingly found higher than expected angular distributions of the 12C alpha particles. The issue remains unresolved and we provide an explanation based on a novel, exotic process involving the 20Ne Hoyle state.

A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we apply this concept to a sample of 13 stars that host terrestrial planets similar to our Sun, utilising high-precision data on their elemental composition. Based on this and other constraints, we simulated the detailed mineral makeup and internal structures of hypothetical habitable-zone exoplanets around these stars. Our model indicates that most of these planets are expected to have compositions and internal structures analogous to those of Earth. However, our analysis reveals two exceptions, the Kepler-10 and Kepler-37 planets, which would likely develop cores significantly smaller than Earth due to oxidation. Furthermore, our exploration of this devolatilisation model's boundaries and variation in planetary mass and size highlights the potential diversity of internal structures in terrestrial planets. By combining precise star abundances, devolatilisation, and planetary mass and size considerations, our study advances understanding of terrestrial exoplanet interior structures, which are pivotal in grasping planetary evolution and dynamics.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict the potential of channel representation learning by the DNN. This research suggests attention-based CSI for learning robust features. The proposed approach's efficacy in centralized and distributed massive MIMO systems is assessed using ray-tracing channels in two railway environments under varying conditions, resulting in a superior performance compared to a conventional DNN.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors.

We investigate functions defined on the vertices of the Hamming graphs H(n,q), focusing specifically on those with support contained in the direct sum of the eigenspaces U_i(n,q), U_j(n,q), and U_k(n,q) for indices j < k. By establishing a one-to-one correspondence between these functions and those with support in U_j(n,q), we determine the functions with minimal support, and use this result to calculate the functions' values on U_i(n,q) and U_k(n,q), resulting in new identities. Applying these identities, we compute the 13th moment of the adjacency matrix of H(n,q), and use this to calculate the 13th moment of the adjacency matrix of the projective Hamming graph H(n+1,q), resolving a previously partially studied issue.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables running tasks available in the original software within a browser. It offers a basic model upload feature and a server-loaded model option, providing web access to existing models. Users can access ShinyCOPASI at http://shiny.copasi.org/ and the source code at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified uncertainty quantification framework approximating various physical quantities is developed. This approach combines multiple uncertainty models, enabling the separation of distinct uncertainty sources. Furthermore, a novel sparse sampling method is proposed to evaluate the combined effect of different uncertainty models. The performance of this framework is assessed against benchmark problems by comparing predicted variances with actual values.

We are investigating quantum group analogues of the free group factors' radial subalgebras, specifically those of class functions, within the context of compact quantum groups. We found that the algebras of class functions for the free orthogonal quantum groups cannot be maximally abundant *-subalgebras (MASAs) under certain conditions. Central to our research is the concept of quasi-split inclusions. We demonstrated that the inclusion of the class functions' algebra is quasi-split if the given quantum group is unipotent, thereby providing an alternative explanation for a previous finding. Additionally, we established connections between the MASD-structure of these algebras and the central structures of classical free group factors, including the existence of certain faithful, semi-faithful, and tracially faithful embeddings. We have also discovered specific examples related to Fibonacci quantum groups, which possess unique properties, such as having a dual group that is not symmetric.

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a general framework for large-scale convex-concave saddle-point problems, can be employed. By leveraging its parameters, inexact policy iteration offers a starting point for large-scale policy evaluation, utilizing value function approximation or multi-step transfer techniques, and ultimately leads to efficient policy optimization via the exponentiated gradient method. Experimental results validate its superiority over traditional policy iteration and state-of-the-art methods for policy optimization.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior.

This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. To efficiently handle the large datasets produced by such simulators, an approach involves first selecting key points to approximate the output, and then applying a specialized method to estimate optimal input parameters at those points, while accounting for any uncertainty in the solution. A comprehensive simulation-based study compares the proposed technique with other established methods on a range of synthetic and real-world scenarios.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and considering the influence of random example exposure, according to Gourdeau et al. (2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first distribution-free algorithms for achieving robustness, leveraging both local membership and equivalence queries. Our results are particularly notable as they demonstrate that the use of local queries can significantly enhance robust model evaluation, requiring only slightly more equivalence queries, without needing any new distributional assumptions. We further investigate the value of local equivalence queries in combination with membership queries, developing an algorithm that shows robustness can be achieved even in the presence of malicious data, with the additional requirement of distribution knowledge for parameter estimation.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV and within a narrow angle to the photon. By pairing with a high-transverse-momentum photon, the trajectory of the jet is well constrained. This allowed the comparison of jet fragmentation functions in proton-proton and lead-lead collisions, both as a function of the jet rapidity and in relation to charged particles in the jet. This comparison was made over several regions of the jet. In central lead-lead collisions, the modification of the fragmentation functions is significant, with alterations in the shape and yield of the fragmentation functions, particularly for particles with low transverse momentum. However, this modification is minimal in collisions that occur outside the central region of the collision.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts.

Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, has yielded an assortment of peculiar attributes for the object. New images taken by Keck/MOSFIRE and HST/WFC3 cameras have established that the object is among a select few with extremely faint proper motion, indicating it has a very low temperature consistent with the coolest Y dwarfs. Moreover, the object possesses color indices of W1-W2 and ch1-ch2 about 1.6 mag bluer than a typical Y dwarf. New data collected from WISE, Spitzer, and HST for parallax measurement have determined a close distance of $16.3^{+1.4}_{-1.2}$ parsecs and a substantial transverse velocity of $207.4{\pm}15.9$ km/s. The calculated J, W2, and ch2 absolute magnitudes align with the coolest Y dwarfs despite W1-W2 and ch1-ch2 indices displaying a distinct divergence. Research suggests that the object is most likely an ancient metal-poor substructure member of the Milky Way, specifically belonging to the Galactic halo, and is most similar to YCSJ0246+4949 in terms of its spectral and photometric characteristics. Due to its bright magnitude, the object is amenable to spectroscopic examination; as such, it holds great potential to shed light on the chemical composition of

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions with
similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric parameters and 
system size, while examining the influence of final-state interactions. Results show that 
transverse momentum spectra do not diverge significantly and that $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields 
are similar within 10-15\% uncertainty across various collisions. Also, the average 
radial transverse momentum was found to increase linearly with the number of charged particles.

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points, making it cost-effective by utilizing modern computer hardware. Our proposal incorporates an innovative technique to handle flavor transitions, enabling rapid evaluation of PDFs and their higher-order derivatives. Moreover, we outline a strategy for constructing NNLO DPDFs, emphasizing the significance of flavor-separation terms.

Specimens made of Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, in the form of cylinders, were created using a combination of saltwater and heat, and then fired at various temperatures to analyze their internal structure, strength and contraction. The internal structures of these materials were studied under a microscope and their mechanical properties were tested using a universal testing machine. The experiment was performed twice using different types of simulants for Martian and Lunar soil, resulting in manufactured samples resembling traditional building blocks and the initial stages of 3D printing with a binder. The results indicated that the optimal firing temperature for both types of simulants lies between 1100 C and 1200 C. The compressive strength of these materials met the requirements for building structures on other planets, suggesting their potential for use as building materials in extraterrestrial construction and as a base material for additive manufacturing processes similar to 3D printing with a binder.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This study provides a theoretical analysis of perturbations in a liquid film surrounding a fiber, taking into account variations in the liquid-solid interface due to roughness or other factors. The model considers two scenarios: one where slip is negligible, and another with slip that follows Stickler's law. By applying the Stokes equation and combining it with conservation of momentum, the results reveal how roughness influences the velocity and pressure fields around the fiber. The model is then used to investigate perturbation growth, and the findings are compared with existing experimental data.

A novel technique has been developed for estimating a star formation rate (SFR) based on the emission of a specific hydrogen line called the Brackett-$\gamma$ (Br$\gamma$). This technique leverages a relationship between Br$\gamma$ and H$\alpha$ emissions that can be measured more accurately even at redshifts beyond 6, which is significant for identifying the most distant galaxy candidates. By applying the 15th edition of the Spectral Energy Distribution Template Library, a library of energy distributions developed by P. Cigan, we calculated a line ratio of 0.068 for nearby spiral galaxies with low extinction levels. Furthermore, we considered the effects of two factors on the uncertainty in the SFR estimate: the variability of the line ratio and the line emission itself. By applying these considerations, we created a formula for calculating SFRs based on Br$\gamma$ line fluxes with an associated 0.06 dex uncertainty when applied to diverse galaxy types. This new SFR estimator can potentially contribute to studying star formation at high redshifts and for dusty galaxy populations where other SFR indicators fail.

This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a significant segment of the braided auto-equivalences present in the near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near near

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome that contradicts conventional travelling wave approximations commonly utilised in the field.

This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to classify handwritten mathematical terms. Given that mathematical expressions often encompass multiple terms, such as numbers and operators, within a single text entry, we developed a binary classifier to determine if an entry contains a mathematical term. Leveraging the Cycle-Consistency Loss from cycleGANs, we created a multi-classifier for identifying specific mathematical terms. Our approach combines both classifiers, enabling efficient mathematical term recognition. Notably, we transformed the original 10-classifier into an aggregate model with 13 classes, incorporating an additional class for blank entries to account for potential inaccuracies in the pre-trained word2vec model. Our test results demonstrated high accuracy rates of 0.946 and 0.942 for binary and multi-classification, respectively.
