This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean values, this new approach can model any distribution on a positive real axis. We found that using the median instead of the mean yields better results, enhancing the accuracy of our model. Furthermore, this method enables the generation of new phone units by training a static model, which can then be used to determine the median phone duration. Evaluations revealed that this approach performance matches or surpasses state-of-the-art results on the median and log likelihood measures.

Species distribution analysis often employs abundance data collected through
sampling, yet predictive models frequently assume data are independently
distributed, failing to account for sampling design. Ignoring this issue may lead
to biased parameter estimates and unreliable prediction maps. To address this
limitation, we developed two Bayesian species distribution models that take
into consideration the spatial autocorrelation inherent in abundance data. To
further improve fit, we incorporated a hierarchical error model. Application
of these models to field data in Central China enabled us to evaluate the effect of
sampling schemes on species distribution predictions. Notably, one of the
proposed models compared favorably to the popular MaxEnt approach.

Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Moreover, studies have shown that general practitioners make fewer mistakes in diagnosing skin lesions when guided by imaging. To bridge this gap, our research focuses on creating a diagnostic tool that combines the strengths of human and machine intelligence. We developed an innovative, user-centric, interactive deep learning network, aptly named GuidedNet, which works as follows: 1) A human provides a preliminary diagnosis based on the patient's medical history and visual insights, sharing this information through unannotated images. 2) GuidedNet uses this initial data to produce a diagnosis, accompanied by visual guidance highlighting key areas that contributed to this outcome. We tested GuidedNet using data from The Skin Cancer Foundation, comparing its performance with non-interactive methods and state-of-the-art models. The results show that our network outperforms other methods, demonstrating the significant benefits of collaborative effort in the diagnostic process. Ultimately, we envision a future where human-machine collaborations like GuidedNet help close the gap between available dermatologic care and the ever-growing demand for it.

To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from spectral time series data,
we introduce a probabilistic autoencoder that incorporates a Normalizing Flow module afterword.
Leaning the supernovae's physics allows the model to derive its parameters naturally, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by generating new data samples that mimic the observed spectral evolution pattern.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been observed in a star-forming galaxy located at a distance of 1.8 billion light-years.  The outflow was detected through a technique that analyzes absorption lines across multiple sub-millimeter wavelength data sets.  The outflow's properties include an atomic gas mass of 10 billion solar masses and an outflow rate of 700 solar masses per year.  The outflow's existence is consistent with a pre-existing outflow detected in a nearby less massive gas component and is likely powered by an active galactic nucleus based on the presence of an extremely bright, active central region.  The outflow may play a significant role in preventing the gas from cooling and facilitating star formation by pushing it towards the galaxy's outer edges.  The outflow's properties are comparable to those of extremely luminous galaxies located at much larger distances.  The outflow's atomic gas mass is significantly higher than any previously detected outflow in a galaxy based on similar data sets.  The outflow's existence is consistent with the 'feedback' model that helps explain the diversity of galaxy evolution.

To study the movement of fluid into a swirling, turbulent plume carrying heavy particles, researchers conducted an experiment in a lab setting. The shape of this plume is axisymmetric and the particles within it are suspended in a fluid that starts at a concentrated source. When the direction of the fluid flowing out of the source is altered, changes are observed in the flow characteristics. Specifically, modifying the direction results in changes to the pattern of particles within the plume, affecting their distribution and movement. Notably, the direction of fluid flowing out of the source influences the flow patterns in two distinct ways, depending on whether the direction is generally vertical or vertical with some directional component. When the direction is mainly vertical, the pattern of particles within the plume is characterized by an inner region with little entrainment and an outer region with high entrainment rates. Conversely, when the direction is mostly vertical with some horizontal component, the pattern of particles within the plume changes, potentially leading to changes in the flow dynamics.

Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting hyperedges to model these interactions, we create more comprehensive models, allowing the transmission rate to depend on the number of infectious contacts a person has. This approach leads us to develop new spectral conditions and study various types of contagion models, considering both the mean-field type I and II models and a representation of individual decisions in a probabilistic model. Our study includes numerical examples and the observation that, in some cases, the difference between I and II models can be significant.

Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical calculations, researchers investigated the behavior of spin polarization within the prototype ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayer, which has an in-plane magnetization orientation. Their study reveals that this material exhibits a rich pattern of spin texture within its bulk layers, which is driven by ferromagnetic order and weakened bond phenomenon at the interface. This spin texture phenomenon increases substantially at the interface compared to its inner layers and exhibits a strong dependence on the type of atom involved. This research provides a fundamental understanding of spin cants in 2D magnetic semiconductors and highlights their potential application in the development of spin filters, ferromagnetic interfaces, and devices that modulate spin and valley degrees of freedom.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases: an inertial radius, an asymptotic profile, an inverse rotation belt, and angular momentum loss. 

As stars like the Sun mature, their rotational velocity outwards from the core slows, while inward it accelerates due to differential rotation. This pattern is largely governed by the star's angular momentum distribution, particularly in the outer layers where the inverse rotation belt develops.

In this study, we explore the interaction between this rotation belt and star spots, focusing on the dynamics within a 1.1 solar mass star throughout its 1.5 billion year lifespan under varying external gravitational influences.

We employed 3D simulations of stellar convection using the MGLAM algorithm, resulting in resolved spots with sizes comparable to those observed on the Sun, and tracked their formation and evolution across diverse latitudes, particularly at low and mid-latitudes where the rotation belt prevails.

As the star spins down, spots at low latitudes disappear due to decreased rotation differential, while spots at mid-latitudes rotate faster in the opposite direction. This leads to varying spot lifetimes based on latitude, and consequently, varying activity levels at different latitudes.

This and other studies have simulated complete rotation scenarios for solar-type stars, but instead of solving the equation for rotational velocity, we focused on solving the equation for angular momentum instead, allowing us to include external gravitational influences and predict spot and plage formation, and uuv radiation flux

Deep multimodal learning using K-fan deep Boltzmann machines offers a novel approach to combine multiple input sources. This method can learn a common representation for multiple inputs and is useful for applications like cross-modality image classification and natural language processing. Traditionally, deep Boltzmann machine models were limited by their inability to handle complex, high-resolution data; however, the K-fan model can easily overcome this constraint. In comparison to other state-of-the-art deep multimodal learning methods, the K-fan model outperformed them in various classification tasks, and its representation capability was verified through an analysis of its latent features.

The use of model checking has become increasingly essential in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs. Traditional unit and functional tests are insufficient due to their inability to cover all program execution paths, particularly in detecting synchronization-related issues. Existing verification tools rely on formal specifications, which may not always be available or up-to-date. Leveraging the power of learning techniques, we introduce LCerma, a new model-based testing tool that learns missing program invariants from execution traces. Building upon cerma, a previous machine learning-based tool, LCerma incorporates two improved algorithms to enhance its performance. We also develop a new testing engine, LC-Tester, to utilize the learned invariants in generating test cases. An empirical study using multi-threaded programs from the ThreadSafetyBench suite demonstrates the effectiveness of LCerma and LC-Tester.

The globally predominant messaging app, WhatsApp, boasts a distinct characteristic 
in its closed nature and user-friendly capabilities of transferring multimedia and
large-scale information sharing to groups, making it an ideal breeding ground for 
the spread of pseudoscientific claims. Our research focuses on uncovering the hidden 
patterns within WhatsApp groups that facilitate the dissemination of false conspiracy 
theories. We introduce an innovative web scraping approach, collecting a substantial 
dataset of conversational content from two distinct medical-related WhatsApp groups. 
An in-depth linguistic and semantic analysis is then applied to identify prevalent 
misinformation, evaluate the level of engagement among users, and assess the extent 
of knowledge transfer through the measurement of semantic similarity between messages. 
Our findings reveal significant differences in the conversational patterns of the two 
groups, with the group susceptible to conspiracy theories exhibiting higher levels of 
engagement and linguistic complexity, suggesting that countermeasures aimed at reducing 
the spread of pseudoscientific claims in such groups should prioritize the stimulation of 
critical thinking and clear information dissemination.

We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model, leading to population partitioning into distinct groups based on genetic information. Each group's frequency spectrum can be represented as a collection of non-negative integers representing the number of individuals containing a specific genetic variant, and our findings relate the asymptotic behavior of these collections as the population size grows to the distribution of the total number of groups.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. By selectively amplifying key input characteristics and suppressing irrelevant ones, AReLU enables our system to prioritize artifact-related features. Our proposed system was applied to the logical access task using the ASVSpoof2019 dataset and demonstrated improved performance compared to systems utilizing standard, non-adaptive activation functions.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding.  Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires navigating the constraints on desirable inflationary paths, moduli stabilization to achieve a stable de-Sitter phase, and ensuring the scalars remain heavy compared to the Hubble scale to facilitate single-field inflation.  Additionally, the gravitational wave signatures produced during inflation will soon become detectable by next-generation experiments such as LISA.  We will discuss recent advancements in constructing inflationary models within the K\"ahler-Matter-Coupled Supergravity framework, which includes the effective descriptions of a number of simple scalar potentials.  We will then apply these models to two types of inflationary scenarios: monodromy inflation and complex-axion inflation, while also examining the implications for low-energy physics, and the properties of additional neutral scalar particles that may remain after inflation.

Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs rather than the transmission of light. An experiment was conducted and supported by theoretical findings, showing this nonreciprocity through second-order coherence functions of photon pairs created by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. Changing the direction of the pump's propagation leads to significant diminishment in coherence functions while maintaining the transmission.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in identifying and correcting material flaws affecting coherent quantum operations.

We are looking for infinite cardinals $\kappa$ that allow for a division of the real number line $\mathbb R$ into $\kappa$ unique Borel sets. The well-known Hausdorff solution indicates that $\aleph_1$ sets work in one instance. Our research shows, however, that the size range for these divisions can vary extensively, allowing a specific set of natural numbers $A$ with values 0 and 1 included, to dictate the $\aleph_0$ natural number count of $\kappa$, in turn influencing the number of $\kappa$ natural numbers that satisfy this condition.

In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit the momentum strategies of CTAs for personal profit. In a study, it is demonstrated that these traders indeed undermine CTA performance and the increase in their activity over time directly correlates with the decline in CTA returns. Moreover, it is evident that these short-term traders utilize a 'free-rider' approach, copying the momentum signals from CTA index funds. Interestingly, a small group of high-frequency traders exhibits contrasting behavior, showing improved CTA returns when they participate actively.

Identifying the application protocol is a crucial process in network security monitoring that demands a detailed analysis of network traffic patterns. However, pinpointing the application protocol can be a challenging and laborious task, requiring substantial resources and time. In an effort to automate this process, our research introduces yabeen, an open-source tool designed to accurately identify application protocols across various network services. Leveraging traffic differentiation techniques, yabeen can pinpoint application protocols by analyzing traffic characteristics, thus enhancing efficiency and scalability. To demonstrate its effectiveness, our tool was tested on multiple datasets, revealing issues with nbeeg, a widely-used commercial tool, which failed to correctly identify application protocols in certain instances. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that using the number of processes and flow durations in conjunction with other features yields superior results in distinguishing application protocols.

Electrostatic gating limits the flow of electrons in integrated circuits. Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is difficult to regulate. However, we found that superconducting strips atop thin magnetic films can completely reflect magnons through their magnetic resistance to stray magnetic fields. The significant frequency shifts resulting from this response effectively halt the forward flow of magnons perpendicular to the magnetic field. By positioning two superconducting gates in parallel with the magnetic field, we were able to create a confined magnon system. The added capability to control coherent magnons enables new functionalities, such as transferring magnetization at specific times and generating entangled states.

A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, novel classes emerging from unseen data patterns on various devices challenge this methodology as they are not accessible to the central server or fellow users. In response, we suggest a unified system addressing the associated issues during federated learning. Our system is evaluated in two distinct contexts - 1) when users conceal the new class labels, and 2) when users disclose this information. Our experiment demonstrates that our system successfully detects novel classes both when they are accessible and when they remain hidden.

A comprehensive theoretical model is offered in this paper for analyzing high-dimensional entangled systems, specifically the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. Initially, we apply our approach to measure a complete three-photon GHZ state across three dimensions and then extend it to multi-photon systems within higher dimensional settings. In our model, both hyperentanglement of photons and the quantum Fourier transform are employed. The proposed solution will serve as a useful resource for developing high-dimensional quantum computation and communication.

This research paper delves into the problem of uplink cascaded channel estimation in multi-user multiple-input-single-output systems aided by intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRSs) with variable phase-encoding capabilities. To address this challenge, we present a joint estimation approach for the direct and indirect uplink channels. This proposal involves leveraging the recreational property of positive semidefinite matrices to decompose the joint estimation problem into simpler sub-problems, then designing an iterative algorithm based on the alternating minimization technique. We further introduce a maximum a posteriori (MAP) probability-based estimator to determine the arbitrary variables associated with the IRSs. Simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm, which outperforms the conventional minimum mean squared error (MMSE) method.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information.

The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the modular network structure known as the ESBN, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items outside of its initial training scope, similar to how children can apply what they've learned to new situations.

Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming actions, such as accessing a disk or the network. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less storage and processes information faster. A different solution, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as an expansion of the Bloom filter. A modification to this concept has also been explored, particularly by Dietzfelbinger and Pagh. Their variation reduces storage needs while maintaining similar efficiency as the original Bloomier filter. A filter based on the Bloomier filter's alteration can offer quicker lookup times and need less storage, making it faster and more storage-efficient. This modified storage-efficient filter has both deterministic and probabilistic lookup methods. During lookup operations, a probabilistic approach may be used, similar to standard Bloom filters. For lookup operations that yield false positives, a deterministic method can be employed to verify results with greater accuracy. A key advantage of this design is its ability to support partial matches of sets, including matches for single elements, all elements, or any elements within a specified range. These features enable the detection of patterns within large datasets, such as finding overlapping segments in a large collection of intervals. A key application of this concept is the detection of patterns in large datasets, such as finding overlapping segments in a large collection of intervals.

Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to a significant generalization of a notable result by Edakun. In addition, we establish important inequalities of Brunn-Minkowski and Gauss-Bonnet types. Ultimately, our findings elucidate the essential contribution of holomorphic line bundles to the geometry of projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds.

A new approach aims to derive market trend insights from dynamic price equations, specifically those that describe how future prices converge to optimal values, thereby maximizing trading volume per unit of time. This methodology stands out for its inherent ability to select a suitable time frame, which is automatically identified by analyzing past market activity and determining the state of highest trading efficiency. To facilitate trend analysis, both historical and forecasted price data are considered, with past prices represented by lagging values and forecasted prices represented by advancing values.

This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC clustering algorithm, which creates reliable and separate categories to protect against malicious data submission during the training process. Concurrently, clients create its own model within each category using Mini-Batch MC Dropout. The server then selects a representative model from each cluster through VOT voting process, and subsequently, initiates a new iteration of training. The algorithm enables servers and clients to collaboratively develop robust models by distinguishing legitimate and malicious data without compromising user privacy.

We successfully submitted the winning entry to the NeurIPS 2021 - AWS Deepracer challenge, which required developing a self-driving vehicle model that interacts with its environment through action-reward interactions. The objective was to create an autonomous vehicle model that navigates a simulated track, adapts to real-world settings, and completes a lap at maximum speed while staying on course. The competition was part of The AI Driving Olympics (AI-DO), a series that fosters embodied intelligence advancements in autonomous driving, by benchmarking the progress in applied autonomy. The Deepracer challenge proved to be complex, especially when translating skills from simulated to real-world settings, so we implemented a two-pronged approach to bridge the domain gap in observation spaces by using a style transfer technique and a cutomized training procedure for reinforcement learning policies. By leveraging an institutional knowledge base and fine-tuning models using limited real-world data, we overcame the absence of local training data. The evaluation entailed assessing our model's performance both in simulated and real-world environments.

Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincingly authentic deepfakes, which have sparked interest across multiple sectors due to their vast potential applications, despite raising serious societal and security risks. This chapter examines the advancements and difficulties in the production and identification of deepfakes, and also explores the potential solutions to improve the resilience of deepfake detection for a broad range of media, such as real-world images and videos. Furthermore, it proposes future research directions for tackling deepfake-related issues.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring liquid water oceans, provided they do not possess massive H2/He envelopes that would cause them to be excessively hot. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that observable differences exist between the solubility equilibria and thermochemistry of carbon and nitrogen gases in small vs. massive H2 atmospheres, with the requirement for a liquid water ocean and thermal equilibrium being mutually exclusive. Thermochemical nitrogen gas recycling to the solid state causes inner atmospheric cooling, facilitating the formation of carbon-rich aerosols that absorb UV radiation and increase the energy gap between the planet's dayside and night side. These carbon-rich aerosols could also influence photosynthesis and climate feedbacks on potentially habitable planets, with implications for the search for biosignatures in sub-Neptune exoplanets and their potential habitability.

Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the current and desired output, without necessitating backpropagation. MPN utilizes a 3x3 CNN-like architecture, where triadic synaptic connections between binary neurons facilitate complex sequence memory through asymmetrical connections, enabling efficient information transfer. Our study demonstrates the model's capability to learn various temporal patterns at an impressive pace, outperforming a 21-neuron McCulloch-Pitts circuit.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 322,115
instances from distinct vocabularies, encompassing 4,946 unique words.
The evaluation process focused on distinct vocab word recognition in real-world images.
The submitted predictions showed significant variation among competitors.
The top performer achieved a character accuracy rate of 45.60 and a
word accuracy rate of 36.46 for novel vocabulary words.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating separate solution branches in parameter-dependent systems and generalizes seamlessly to multi-parameter tracking. To demonstrate the proposed methodology, this research achieves the precise calculation of random equilibrium cycles in the Lorenz system, as well as solution branches and 2-dimensional planes of steady states in the Swift-Hohenberg equation.

The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is often impractical due to cost constraints and the associated risk of damage to equipment. Furthermore, industrial systems also exhibit underlying patterns and changes over time, affecting their overall shift detection and forecasting. To address these challenges, this research introduces an innovative two-step method. Firstly, it employs sparse principal component analysis to identify the most informative factors within the data, thus minimizing the need for complete data sets. Subsequently, a multivariate change-point detection approach is used to pinpoint critical time intervals marked by significant changes, followed by the application of forecasting techniques to predict future trends. To evaluate the performance of this method, extensive simulations are conducted across various scenarios. Additionally, the proposed approach is successfully demonstrated on real-world data from industrial air quality monitoring systems, highlighting its utility in practice.

We have created a detailed analysis of the origins and development of two disrupted galaxies that merged with the Milky Way's outer layers: the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 systems. Our sophisticated computational model, designed to simulate galaxy growth patterns, is based on exponential infall scenarios and allows for reliable fitting of these patterns. Our analysis led to the discovery of key timescales for each galaxy: 1.1 billion years for GSE to form and 1.7 billion years for Wukong to form, with both galaxies experiencing infall until 9-10 billion years ago. Prior to this, both galaxies underwent rapid growth, with timescales similar to the cosmic average, but as infall continued, their growth slowed and eventually the galaxies' growth rates decreased more rapidly than average. In contrast, another model that simulated smooth, uninterrupted infall led to significantly different predictions: 2.2 billion years for GSE and 4.1 billion years for Wukong. Our findings are in line with predictions that these galaxies would have experienced star formation similar to the Milky Way's, but as they merged with the Milky Way, their star formation was suppressed and shifted towards lower metallicities due to the galaxies' outer layers being stripped away, with the remaining stars being absorbed into the Milky Way's halo.

Given a profinite group G, an S[[G]]-module is a G-spectrum that fulfills certain criteria, leading to the definition of the homotopy orbit spectrum X_{hG} associated with an S[[G]]-module X. When X's constituents meet specific finiteness criteria, a homotopy orbit spectral sequence arises with an E2-term being the continuous homology of G, taking coefficients from the C-homology of G on the C-part of the spectrum. This sequence converges towards the homotopy homotopy group of X, exhibiting a link between the homotopy homotopy groups of X and X's constituents, displaying an action decomposition.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy.

Researchers used spectroscopic techniques to investigate electronic properties at various interfaces between InAs and EuS. 
In particular, a sharp interface model was tested using photoemission spectroscopy, by comparing it to an experiment where InAs was grown on a EuS-covered substrate using a technique that alters the europium oxide's bonding configuration. 
The results showed that the electronic structure near the surface of the InAs/EuS interface is similar to the free InAs surface. 
Additionally, the study found that the electronic structure of the InAs surface is not significantly altered when it is covered with europium oxide. 
The data suggested that the bonding configuration of a specific europium oxide layer is responsible for aligning the electronic structures of InAs and EuS. 
The findings are supportive of previous research and open up new possibilities for further investigation into the electronic properties of InAs/EuS interfaces.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, such intricate models necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and resources for processing speed. In this research, we introduce ClickTrain, a proposal for efficiently training and fine-tuning modern CNNs on standard hardware. ClickTrain leverages the parallelism capabilities of commodity GPUs via a multi-node Slurm cluster setup, allowing for the division of models into clickable components and simultaneous training of these components in parallel. Our results demonstrate that ClickTrain can successfully train and fine-tune ResNet-50 and MobileNetV2 models approximately 3 to 5 times faster than conventional methods.

This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying duality principles, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus has a Kripke model, if it adheres to a specific structural rule. Furthermore, we establish a dual relationship between certain mathematical structures, specifically modal algebras and topological Kripke spaces, utilizing a topological model developed from Priestley spaces.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates rapid and accurate estimation of the parameters governing the gravitational wave signal. This necessitates a swift and effective matching algorithm within a Bayesian search method that utilizes a signal model and can handle weak signals over varying frequencies. We have developed such an algorithm by adapting the template-based search method to accommodate binary neutron star and neutron star-black hole signals. By testing this method in simulated data, we have demonstrated its efficacy in detecting binary neutron star and neutron star-black hole events, even at low signal strengths.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star called TOI-5542 approximately every 75 days. Initially detected by the TESS satellite, the exoplanet, which has a radius similar to that of Jupiter, has been further confirmed using data from ground-based spectrographic equipment. Analysis of this data has shown that the exoplanet, which has an estimated mass roughly equivalent to that of Jupiter, likely formed through migration or by being ejected from a binary star system. Further research has found evidence of a second, smaller planet, which has an estimated mass roughly a tenth that of Jupiter and orbits around the star every 5.5 days, suggesting that the system may be home to three planets in total.

Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs for the development of optimal operational strategies: they are often characterized by an extremely vast number of states and actions, as well as a difficult-to-compute transition matrix. To resolve these challenges, we develop an algorithm that combines policy iteration with subgradient ascent. We show that this approach allows the CMDP to converge to a solution at a rate proportional to $O(\log(T)/\sqrt{T})$, where T represents the number of iterations, provided that a specific condition is met. This method also offers an efficient way to reduce the dimensionality of the CMDP by exploiting its structural properties when applicable. We successfully demonstrate its efficacy in two real-world problems: multi-product inventory control with a limited capacity and dynamic network flow control.

This research outlines a multi-layered approach to recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols, considering their inherent complexity and varied shapes. Breaking down the symbols into basic components like strokes and symbols is akin to segmenting a tree structure. Identifying these components proves to be a challenge due to the inherent variability in handwritten scripts. An efficient method using the $k$-nearest neighbors for classifying stroke characteristics and symbol analysis via a Conditional Random Field is proposed to address this issue. Furthermore, a novel stroke segmentation algorithm based on the similarity of dynamic binarization and similarity of a symbol's components is introduced. In specific, the application of the $k$-NN algorithm results in an accuracy of 68% for this task. In contrast to traditional approaches, which often rely on pre-defined rules, this novel method dynamically determines the segmentation boundaries for each symbol based on its visual features. A comprehensive dataset called 'MATH' comprising over 100,000 instances, categorized into training, validation, and testing sets, is developed to support and demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. When evaluated on the 'MATH' dataset, the proposed method achieved remarkable recognition accuracy and outperformed even the best basic feature-based method by a significant margin of 10%.

A geometric interpretation is provided for superconformal quantum mechanics based on a hyper-Kahler cone that is the result of combining several copies of a symplectic 2-dimensional torus. The phase space of this theory is equivalent to the union of the odd Dolbeault cohomology classes of certain twisted sections on the cone. The spectrum of BPS states can be represented by the twisted Dolbeault cohomology classes of the unrolled cone. The excitation of BPS states is described as a shift in degree for a specific class of sheaves on the cone. Utilizing this framework, an explicit formula is developed for the Hamiltonian of superconformal quantum mechanics based on this model.

We examine the impact of network architecture on disease propagation in theoretical models of complex networks, comparing non-homogeneous and homogeneous network scenarios. A numerical model, inspired by the Manwaring-Liu equation, is developed to analyze the effect of the network's degree distribution on epidemic prevalence. Our results demonstrate that the relationship between the epidemic's spreading speed and the network's clustering coefficient is inversely proportional, indicating that the likelihood of an epidemic spreading rapidly is significantly lower in clustered networks. Conversely, we observe an increase in epidemic outbreaks in networks characterized by a wide distribution of node degrees.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithms are commonly used for solving complex decision-making problems. However, their convergence can be slow, especially in challenging tasks. Integrating these algorithms with a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) approach offers several benefits, primarily due to HMC's ability to leverage the target distribution's geometry to make more efficient sampling movements. By incorporating this geometric guidance, HMC can serve as a driver of advanced exploratory actions. Building upon this concept, we develop two HMC-based modifications of actor-critic algorithms: the HamAC-RND and the HamSAC. The HamAC-RND algorithm combines the actor-critic method with HMC-driven action exploration, while the HamSAC algorithm applies HMC in a variety of initial policy distributions. The results of our experiments demonstrate that both HamAC-RND and HamSAC algorithms outperform their traditional actor-critic counterparts, in particular by significantly boosting the performance on difficult tasks.

It's widely recognized that any prime number $p$ greater than $5$ can be represented as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. We will refer to the set of numbers with the former form as $A$, and the set of numbers with the latter form as $B$. In this investigation, the interplay between the sets $A$ and $B$ is explored through an analysis of the sums of products of elements from these sets, specifically under the mod $p$ reduction of integers.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. Scenarios such as fog, dust, or extreme lighting conditions can impair regular sensing technologies or make them excessively expensive to implement. We introduce a novel, cost-effective method utilizing only audio signals to create a reliable mapping system within limited CPU resources, even in partially opaque environments. Our proposed system generates 3D maps based on real-time acoustic source localization and is capable of operating on low-cost devices, where processing a single frame takes approximately 8.8 milliseconds. Comprehensive experiments were conducted both on simulated data and in real-world settings, demonstrating that our acoustic mapping system can function optimally in partially obscured conditions, significantly outperforming other methods when evaluating mapping accuracy, audio quality, and computational efficiency.

Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that can be spectroscopically analyzed, exhibits an irregular orbit. Our analysis focuses on Nereid's spectral characterization utilizing its reflectance spectrum between 0.8-2.4 $\mu m$, particularly in the unexplored 0.8-1.4 $\mu m$ range, as we attempt to identify the spectral absorption features that correspond to its icy composition. Our findings indicate the presence of crystalline water ice, coinciding with existing observations. Nonetheless, using simple models consisting of intimate water ice mixtures, we fail to attain a comprehensive match of absorption bands, especially considering the spectral continuum, at the wavelengths of 1.5 and 2.0 $\mu m$. This could be resolved by accounting for both crystalline and amorphous water ice, as well as taking into account the influence of sub-micron grain sizes. Furthermore, combining magnetite with components of the CM2 chondrite Murchison offers a feasible framework for understanding the spectral variations among objects like Nereid, particularly in those with neutral-sloped spectra. It's worth noting that magnetite provides a fitting explanation of Nereid's spectral continuum, eliminating the necessity of incorporating Tholin-like organic substances. Our analysis also reveals that non-ice components of outer solar system bodies may closely resemble those found in carbonaceous chondrites, as proposed for Halley's comet (

Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of order $n \geq 2$, consisting of elements from the finite field $F(q)$ of order $q \geq 2$. Additionally, let $V_{2n}(q)$ be the free left module of its counterpart ${^2T_n(q)}$. Studies have proven that over the projective line based on $T_n(q)$, we find $(q+1)^{(n-1)}q^{\frac{3(n-1)(n-2)}{2}}$ affine planes of order $q$, where points in such a plane correspond to the non-free cyclic submodules in $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$, while lines consist of non-isomorphic rank $k$ cyclic submodules in $\mathcal{R}_k(q)$, for $1 \leq k \leq n-1$.

In a 1986 paper in J. Symbolic Logic, Pawlikowski demonstrated that under specific conditions regarding Cohen and random reals, certain model properties can be inferred within extensions of those models. This is proven through a novel application of Tukey-order with models, expanding upon an existing concept introduced by Vojtáš in 1991. By leveraging this notion, it can be shown that certain model properties can imply each other, thereby establishing key theorems related to random and Cohen reals within these models.

A new pessimism-based Bayesian approach aims to develop reliable dynamic treatment regimes (DTRs) by utilizing historical data from multiple studies, while considering the uncertainty associated with each treatment's effectiveness in each study. To achieve this goal, the algorithm constructs a posterior distribution for the optimal policy by sampling treatment regimes that are unlikely to be suboptimal according to each study's Bayesian estimate. As the algorithm updates its knowledge, it refrains from inferring high-probability suboptimal regimes. After converging to a stable state, the algorithm outputs a reliable policy that is also robust to changes in future data. Our simulation experiments demonstrate that this method can create generalizable DTRs that perform well across multiple scenarios, even when the contexts are different from those used to train the model. In one practical application, the algorithm was used to develop a DTR for patients with diabetes, leveraging data from multiple research projects, and the resulting policy was implemented in clinical practice.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be defined by the relationship to Wakamatsu tilting bimodules, with specific cases yielding known dualities. When restricting these relationships to subcategories of finitely generated modules with particular dimensions, previously established correspondences and dualities on tilting modules are reaffirmed. The implications of this relationship include demonstrating equivalences of derived categories of finitely generated Gorenstein-projective modules, as well as the invariance of certain algebraic invariants under tilting transformations.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's 120 vertices and edge directions associated with the E8 root system. This configuration's invariance under the E8 group's 504 movements ensures that all physical observables are invariant to these transformations.

In a flat band superconductor, bosonic modes can freely propagate whereas unpaired electrons are fixed in place. To study this highly interacting system, we developed a family of Hamiltonians describing flat band superconductors, applying a sequence of symmetry-preserving deformations to the exact many-body wavefunction. These deformations mix different symmetries, allowing us to analyze the effects of spin-orbit coupling, inter-band coupling, and lattice deformations on the exact wavefunction. Our findings indicate that bosonic modes can be manipulated through all aforementioned perturbations, whereas unpaired electrons remain unaffected. By applying these deformations to the Sr$_2$FeO$_3$ slab, we demonstrate the potential to control energy, momentum, and spin-momentum locking of bosonic modes at the surface, showing that electrons at the core can still be coupled to these modes via exchange. Our study paves the way for the exploration of flat band superconductors with precise control over bosonic modes.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a-adic solenoids for which this relationship holds, effectively proving a theorem analogous to the generalized Polya theorem. This proof relies on solving a functional equation for a specific class of functions associated with the character group of the a-adic solenoid.

Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches can be utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of local independence, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance, or applying continuous data methods to the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances. These clustering methods vary conceptually and cannot easily be compared theoretically. To address this, we conduct an in-depth comparative analysis through simulation studies grounded in models for species distribution to evaluate their respective performances. 

This study has been accepted for publication in an upcoming publication titled "Innovations in multivariate statistical modelling: navigating theoretical and multidisciplinary domains," part of Springer Emerging Topics in Statistics and Biostatistics, edited by Ferreira, J., Bekker, A., Arashi, M., and Chen, D.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. This paper proposes an efficient and unified structure that integrates cross-attention context extraction to effectively tackle both tasks. Our approach consists of an optional attention module added to existing salient object detection networks to enhance their performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on multiple datasets in terms of metrics such as Pearson's correlation coefficient, structural similarity index, and salient object detection score. Notably, our approach possesses an advantage in terms of number of parameters compared to existing methods.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants.

A number, N, can be termed a palindrome if its binary format is symmetrical. In this paper, the relationship between the quotients of these symmetrical numbers is explored and several fundamental questions about the resulting sets of integers and fractions are answered. We demonstrate the feasibility of solving this problem using a high-performance computer, which we accomplish by utilizing a parallel algorithm capable of handling a substantial number of symmetrical numbers within a predetermined range.

In an online community of physicists working with X-rays, a relevant topic was discussed: "What are the limitations of using polychromatic X-ray sources in medical and astronomical imaging?" A thorough explanation was provided, highlighting the potential distortions caused by partial energy absorption, sample composition, and varying photon attenuation. An illustrative code example was offered to facilitate further exploration and visualization of these effects.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training leading Handwritten Text Recognition models without the need for line segmentation. Thorough evaluation and analysis affirm the efficacy of the proposed solution.

We have developed a novel storage approach that significantly decreases memory requirements in high-precision atomic nucleus computations. By analyzing energy spectra, we found that a large majority of the nuclear wavefunction's energy contributions come from a limited range of higher-energy elements. We created an algorithm that identifies and utilizes these significant energy contributions, leading to a more efficient method. Compared to existing standard methods, our approach results in a remarkable reduction in storage needs – for instance, we saw a 9,000-times decrease in storage needs for calculating a specific set of nuclei. We successfully implemented this new approach in the nuclear physics computational framework SNAC and achieved a notable CPU speed improvement.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method involves the use of a 'zigzag' integral, similar to a conventional string worldsheet correlation function. The generalization of the amplitude for arbitrary n graviton supermultiplets at two-loop level was also obtained. Additionally, we proposed a formula for arbitrary n at three-loop level and explored its expansion for four graviton supermultipits.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access. Despite this, a few applications still require such programming paradigms. This paper presents an approach to optimize such programs by identifying patterns in memory usage across multiple objects and transforming the code to take advantage of SIMD operations, thus improving performance. This pattern-based SIMD optimization technique was tested on a range of benchmarks and demonstrated the possibility of achieving performance similar to custom low-level code, especially for programs with small data sets. This approach can also facilitate the development of parallel algorithms by automatically transforming sequential code, as shown by practical examples.

We introduce family universal $U(1)_X$ models incorporating three right-handed neutrinos into the Standard Model, utilizing three simple gauge symmetry breaking conditions to define $U(1)_X$. By incorporating an inert doublet, we propose a relativistic dark matter candidate that violates lepton number conservation under certain conditions, thereby making it an ideal early universe reheating agent. Furthermore, we establish the applicable parameter spaces for neutrino mass generation via the seesaw mechanism and, in addition to naturally inducing a small $\mu_W$, obtain a desired Higgs mass. Our work also lays out the viable parameter spaces for consistent $Z_2$-symmetric dark matter behavior and potential signatures related to neutrino mass.

A specific measurement technique must be used for assessing the mechanical characteristics of straw tubes designed for charged particle detection, operating in a vacuum environment. The underlying equations that govern straw behavior when subjected to internal pressure are documented, alongside the introduction of an experimental approach in this paper to investigate strained, pressurized straw tubes. The presented research also focuses on measuring the Poisson's ratio of the straw wall for the NA62 RICH detector, with the ultimate goal of determining the minimum pre-tension required for the straw's structural stability.

In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in the form of credal Bayesian networks, which are parametric models representing the unknown environment with confidence intervals on key variables. Focusing on the 'Maximum Marginal Probability' (MARmax) issue – the maximum possible error probability when misclassifying data, given varying parameter possibilities – our approach transforms MARmax into a more manageable problem on a probabilistic circuit with restrictions. Utilizing an efficient simplification, we provide a theoretically grounded upper limit to MARmax, calculated within linear time relative to the circuit's size, and our experiments demonstrate that this bound is usually precise, and our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of efficiency.

In a supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate with a spin-orbit coupling, an accelerated impurity atom exhibits oscillations that mirror Bloch oscillations in solid matter, despite causing condensate excitements that give rise to internal phonon modes. However, these oscillations have no impact on the condensate's roton minimum position, thereby preserving its periodic matter wave pattern. Notably, the oscillations fade primarily due to wavepacket dispersal; yet, by assuming the impurity behaves as a bright soliton, the decay can be largely countered.

In a generalised quadrangle, a code is a subset of the vertices with its minimum distance determined by the shortest path between distinct elements. The elements of this subset are divided into distinct sets based on their distance from the code. Given the quadrangle's graph has a diameter of four, both the minimum distance and maximum distance from a vertex to its closest code element cannot exceed four. If the minimum distance is four, it signifies the code is a partial ovoid or partial spread; a code is fully classified as an ovoid or spread if it also has a maximum distance of two. A neighbour-transitive code is defined as having an automorphism group that transitively acts on both the code and its closest neighbouring elements. The study focuses on classifying neighbour-transitive codes admitting insoluble automorphisms in thick classical quadrangles, specifically those of distance four. It has been proven that no such neighbour-transitive code exists in a classical quadrangle of thick classical type.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where analysis of the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from ATLASGAL, obtained via the APEX Telescope Large Area Survey of the Galaxy, revealed notable anisotropy in gas density within this area using a two-dimensional correlation function. By identifying the critical angle $\theta_{\rm half}$ and anisotropy parameter $A\equiv \frac{\pi}{4\theta_{\rm half}}-1$, it was determined that gas density in the CMZ is significantly influenced by anisotropic spatial patterns at a scale of approximately 100 parsecs. Wherein, gas density in the northwestern CMZ is more strongly correlated in the northeastern sector. Wherein, gas density is more weakly correlated in the northeastern CMZ compared to the southwestern sector. These findings are consistent with the concept that the CMZ is being shaped by toroidal and spiral structures. Moreover, by examining the mass spectra of molecular complexues within this area it was determined that their distribution is both linear yet fragmented, suggesting that these features are primarily formed as a direct result of the gas density. Furthermore, by comparing with other data it was proposed that the gas density is the defining and primary factor in these features rather than any association with radio jet structures or star clusters. Ultimately, it was suggested that a comprehensive simulation of gas dynamics be conducted in the vicinity of the CMZ

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. Researchers utilizing large-scale X-ray users facilities, such as the XFEL, can study this novel effect yet have failed to demonstrate its application thus far. In this research, we develop a theoretical framework for analyzing fluence-dependent changes in XANES and use it to investigate two model systems, considering both inner-shell and outer-shell excitation. The resulting changes can be categorized into three distinct components: (i) rapid increase due to band mixing; (ii) transient shift resulting from excitation-induced shifts and Fermi level changes; and (iii) alterations stemming from excitation-induced shifts, altered final state lifetimes, and changes in the initial state occupation. The amplitude of fluence-dependent changes is contingent upon the strength of excitation, scaling as the square of the photon flux in the weak excitation limit. In stronger excitation conditions, this relationship ceases to apply. The uniqueness of this novel effect lies in its potential to provide insights into both filled and empty electronic states, as well as the initial state, in highly excited matter. This can facilitate the correlation between XANES and transmission or electron

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS inverter to generate a temperature-dependent reference current, which is then analyzed using statistical methods to extract accurate temperature coefficients. The design, optimized for a 40nm technology, offers high accuracy and reliability, alongside its ability to operate in dynamic voltage and frequency conditions. The results demonstrate the feasibility of this design for chip-scale thermal monitoring, with a precision of $\pm$1.1$\copyright$_P$ and a power consumption of 1.08$\mu$W.

Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new technique is introduced to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead utilizing a continuous wave approach facilitated by a macroscopically distinct joint polarization state shared between two cavities. By leveraging a controllable parameter-driven quantum gate operation, entangled states can be produced from the localized joint polarization state even in the presence of decoherence. We have successfully applied this method to create all three types of polarization entangled states: the Entanglement of Racah algebra, the Entanglement of Wigner rotation and the Entanglement of spin. This research paves the way for implementing a wide array of quantum operations, making it a valuable resource for future quantum information applications.

This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Our study focuses on the competitive ratio of online t-spanners for these point sequences and establishes lower bounds on this ratio for specific algorithms, such as the popular delta-Algorithm. Specifically, we show that no online Algorithm with a competitive ratio better than R^d can be better than the existing Algorithm with a competitive ratio of R^(1+1/n) in one dimension, R^(1+1/n^2) in two dimensions, and R^(1+1/n^d) in d dimensions for any sequence of points. This lower bound holds even when the algorithm has perfect knowledge of future points in the sequence. Additionally, we show that no online Algorithm with a competitive ratio better than R^d can be better than the existing Algorithm with a competitive ratio of R^(1+1/n) in one dimension, R^(1+1/n^2) in two dimensions, and R^(1+1/n^d) in d dimensions for any sequence of points in R^d that is chosen randomly and independently. This lower bound holds even when the algorithm has perfect knowledge of future points in the sequence and that sequence is randomly and independently chosen.

Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a critical requirement, with implications extending to security and data protection aspects. Research has shown that machine learning methods can efficiently classify IoT devices, but these devices frequently undergo changes in behavior due to modifications in their parameters. These alterations often affect the classifier's performance, necessitating frequent updates. Recent research using supervised learning approaches has focused on utilizing network traffic features for classifier training and selection. Nonetheless, these strategies overlook the costs associated with feature extraction and classification, which may be significant in certain scenarios, such as when dealing with the classification of a large number of IoT devices or features that necessitate extensive computation. In this research, we propose an innovative feature selection framework based on wrapper technique, taking into consideration both feature extraction and classification costs. The research also introduces a novel cost-based feature ranking method, where each step relies on a random forest classifier trained with random features to minimize the impact of random forest's own feature selection bias. Additionally, we incorporate a feature subset reduction technique to refine the feature set and enhance the accuracy of our approach. Our experiments using IoT devices, specifically those from Berkeley's Univeristy's Berkeslab, reveal that the proposed method achieves superior results, with an average accuracy of 97.91%, while significantly reducing feature set size (10%) and feature extraction cost.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, to provide multiple semantics for the logics. The study specifically examines the duality between these finite Godel algebras and forests, as well as the concrete semantics resulting from the forest frames, in relation to the standard Kripke semantics for modal logics. The research provides a comparison between the intutionistic modal logic's semantics and the prelinear version's semantics, showcasing the distinctive features of the latter. The study concludes by establishing a correspondence between the finite Godel algebras and the finite forests, and suggests additional research areas, including the extension of the study to infinite structures and the exploration of categories to represent infinite Godel algebras and their respective forest frames.

This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in terms of alignment metrics, such as accuracy or F-score, our approach delivers results equivalent to GIZA++ when trained on a dataset 22 times smaller. Crucially, the method's domain-agnostic training capabilities enable 'on-the-fly' application on any new pair of sentences without requiring extensive retraining.

We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. To assess the likelihood of detecting primordial black holes using PopSyCLE, we modified the code to simulate observables relevant to dark matter searches, while also adjusting the simulation parameters to reflect current limitations in our understanding of dark matter. Our analysis demonstrates that even with present technological capabilities, it is possible to rule out a significant portion of the primordial black hole population as a potential contributor to dark matter. However, the dataset from the Microlensing Telescope Network can be utilized to exclude an even broader range of primordial black hole masses, thereby refining our understanding of the parameter space in which dark matter consisting of these black holes may exist. Moreover, future surveys with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory will enable a substantially expanded range of mass and density spectrum probed, potentially leading to more precise constraints on the PBH mass spectrum.

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter $d$. The systems' phases were studied as a function of parameter $d$ and the packing density of molecules $\eta$, under the condition that only repulsive interactions were present. This led to the system's behavior being controlled solely by the entropy of molecular arrangement. For systems where the packing density was below $0.5$, in addition to the standard liquid state, we observed standard nematic and smectic A liquid crystalline phases. Conversely, when the packing density exceeded $0.5$, two distinct non-standard polar crystalline phases emerged alongside the non-polar hexagonal crystal structure, namely the antiferroelectric splay crystal and the ferroelectric splay crystal. In order to study all of these configurations, we evaluated their characteristics in terms of the parameters representing nematic, smectic, and hexatic ordering, along with the radial distribution function of molecules and the correlation of polarization within these configurations.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates how to conduct such an expansion while preserving (strict) positive definiteness. The study provides a unified explanation for recurring patterns in classification problems involving the invariance of groups, such as distinguishing between periodic functions, classification of stochastic processes, and identifying the covariance functions of stationary processes on the sphere. The findings have significant implications for relevant applications in signal processing and the classification of geometric objects.

A conventional imaging scenario hinges on three essential elements: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest; a detector capable of sensing this scattered light; and a processor tasked with interpreting the received data. Although quantum measurement limitations are negligible in conventional imaging contexts, they may pose significant obstacles when attempting to image sensitive sources, such as individual photons. To overcome this challenge, researchers are exploring the potential of using correlated photon pairs as a light source. By leveraging the coherence of these pairs, not only can the detection process be manipulated, but so can the underlying signal, effectively allowing the detection process to be optimized. This study showcases a hybrid approach that integrates the coherence of photon pairs and the post-selection technique to develop a template-matching algorithm for single-photon detection. The proposed method is capable of processing and reconstructing both one-dimensional and two-dimensional spectra from raw data, and has been successfully validated through experiments.
