Many software systems have adjustable settings through run-time options, such as input parameters, allowing users to modify them to fulfill different purposes, such as reducing the system's footprint or improving security, yet these configurations often go unused in a specific system instance. In our research, we explored an approach called instant specialization, which reduces a software system's configurable aspects by replacing them with fixed values based on the best practices in the field. We applied instant specialization to 13 widely used open-source systems, revealing a significant impact on the systems' binary size and performance, especially after optimization. Notably, the specialization led to a notable average reduction of 21% in binary size and 48% in execution speed, along with improved compression by 42% and a 35% decrease in text and 29% in binary size when considering code obfuscation. Furthermore, we observed fewer errors in specialized binaries, indicating better compiled code. The results show that instant specialization can be an effective technique for creating optimized, binary systems with improved properties.

Light dark matter particles, particularly those weighing less than a GeV, offer an attractive option over heavier, weakly-interacting massive particles. Directly detecting such lightweight particles, however, poses a significant challenge. But if the recoil of a struck nucleus leads to electron ionization, even if the recoil itself is too subtle to be measured, it could still be possible to detect the released electron. This process has been shown to offer a sensitive new way to detect low-mass dark matter. In the present study, a detailed analysis was carried out of the effectiveness of this approach, using accurate calculations of the associated differential rate to predict future detector prospects. It is shown that, for masses around 100 MeV, large, underground laboratories' experiments may now be starting to explore the relevant zone, while those same experiments, along with particle beam facilities, will soon be able to cover the entire relevant mass range.

This paper proposes a method to produce the most connected pairs of qubit states
via an anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction system, resulting in maximally entangled
anti-polariton qubits. The study finds that in the initial product state of two
two-level jitters, an anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction system develops an entanglement
level that mirrors the classic Rabi oscillations seen in such interactions, thus
enabling the creation of maximally connected states. Importantly, the study demonstrates
that even minor losses can still yield near-maximally connected anti-polariton qubits
by adjusting the time of anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction. In doing so, the potential
of anti-Jaynes-Cummings systems is highlighted as a reliable and versatile tool for
generating highly connected entangled states, even in systems prone to losses.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and sports medical analysis have encountered similar challenges. To overcome this challenge, we have developed an advanced IBI estimation technique based on a dual-filter approach. By using an adaptive bidirectional Kalman filter to separate the true ECG signal from the noisy accumulation signal, we can eliminate motion noise and extract the IBIs. Experiments have shown that our technique can accurately estimate IBIs in various real-world conditions.

We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confinement. Analytical calculations of the rate function are done for the free particle in any dimension using a saddle-point expansion. Additionally, a direct numerical approach via solution of the AOUP equations is performed, alongside a method using Legendre-Fenchel transform of the scaled cumulant generating function obtained via a cloning algorithm. Results for the free particle exhibit asymptotically linear behavior on both sides, dependent on a multiplicative factor of the dimension. Confined particles reveal a distinct phase change at an activator-parameters driven transition, characterized by a change in the rate function's sign. This phase change is observed to both increase magnitude and shift phase for the rate function in the confined scenario.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. Unlike other human body datasets, HUMBI captures five fundamental signal types - facial expressions, speech, hand gestures, posture, and eye movements - to provide a more complete understanding of human communication. The dataset features 40,000 synthesized images and 12,000 real-world photos, rendered in five distinct views. The complex transformation from 3D to 2D leads to challenges in reconstructing pose from the provided single-view images. Our Indirect Human Body Reconstruction approach addresses this issue by using volume rendering. The results demonstrate HUMBI's potential to enhance indirect human body reconstruction and provide a fundamental framework for human body expression analysis. The full dataset can be accessed at https://humbi-data.github.io.

Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data labeling, development time, and expertise. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task-specific labels and can transfer entire neural models across languages with minimal adjustments, be they neural networks or rule-based models. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by successfully fine-tuning a neural language model trained on English to produce accurate results in multiple other languages, including Spanish, French, and Hindi, and show that models trained this way compare favorably to strong baselines in terms of performance.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we enhance BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our modified model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving improved PSNR and SSIM scores on the REDS dataset, with a notable reduction in parameter count. Our code is available on the PyTorch hub.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios.

We have improved the performance of heat engines working within specific timeframes, employing a time-varying energy function in conjunction with experimentally grounded limitations on the system's interaction with the thermal bath. A broadly applicable method enables precise optimization of any given protocol subject to these constraints, highlighting the significance of temporal scaling models in achieving enhanced efficiency. When the system's Hamiltonian comprises only a harmonic component, our approach successfully reproduces the optimal performance predicted by the maximum entropy production principle. For complex Hamiltonians involving any type of interaction, we have developed a supplementary strategy to accurately identify the most efficient protocols themselves, even in scenarios where the universal scaling model doesn't apply. These improved protocols demonstrate the robustness of our theoretical framework and its potential for widespread application.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are calculated using a simulated model of the 2000-bus Texas power system superimposed onto an actual map of the region. Simulation results indicate that power substations experiencing storm surge-related flooding may incur additional losses as the hurricane continues to move inland.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify key properties of these maps, including their ability to cover entire domains in a finite number of iterations and have non-integrable invariant measures, potentially leading to long-term chaotic behavior.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at various energy levels.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded auxiliary network is designed to model long-distance dependencies and external frequency features. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate its effectiveness in producing pseudo pitch symbols and generating high-quality audio samples with the help of a pitch generator, particularly when the target pitch lies outside the training frequency range of the baseline WaveNet.

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have become an integral part of our daily lives. However, their limitations become apparent when dealing with unorganized user-item data. In this research, we present a novel framework called LightCF, an approximate algebraic reformulation of MF, to enhance the scalability and efficiency of traditional Matrix Factorization methods. By leveraging a lightweight affinity matrix representation, our method successfully compresses the composable algebraic computation of COMPscomposable algebraic computation of COMPs. This results in substantial memory savings and dramatic speed-ups without compromising accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of LightCF, with a notable 91% reduction in storage requirements on the well-known MovieLens datasets, achieving near-linear scalability with CF-based models, and outperforming the original MF method in terms of both precision and recall. Additionally, LightCF exhibits improved fusion abilities with other CF methods, showcasing its potential as a pre-trained model for various tasks.

Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum by comparing active to quiet periods. By using SDO imagery, we quantified the proportion of active areas (faculae and spots) on the solar surface, independent of previous indicators. These features were linked to variations in solar faculae coverage, as well as the area covered by active regions at solar latitudes below 30deg, which was found to be particularly significant.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperature decreases, its conductance remains relatively insensitive to temperature variations. In contrast, non-Majorana-induced peaks exhibit a typical inverse proportionality relationship between temperature and conductance. We've verified this distinction through numerical simulations, utilizing a one-dimensional Majorana chain with a localized impurity to model the scenario.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Images used in various fields such as social media and computing often require enhancement or editing - a process that can be challenging and often has multiple possible outcomes. In particular, operations like color adjustment and photo blending often lack a definitive result. To address this issue, researchers have developed new techniques involving example-based learning that utilize pairs of input and output images to predict the desired output. However, existing methods are limited to learning pixel-to-pixel relationships and may not consider larger image patterns. In contrast, our proposed model uses input features and automatically selects relevant higher-level relationships through attention mechanisms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model on tasks like color adjustment and photo blending, achieving better results compared to existing methods in all cases.

This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task, recently introduced in the LOVEU challenge at CVPR 2022, where experts faced significant challenges in processing multi-step responses, multiple modalities, and dynamic button representations within video content. To overcome this, we developed a novel context-grounding module that enhances feature mapping using attention mechanisms. We further explored the effects of varying button counts, conducted ablation studies on different network architectures and video feature types, and achieved a 2nd place ranking overall in the LOVEU track 3 competition. Notably, our model demonstrated generalizability across datasets from multiple sources.

This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmosphere's flow patterns and snowflake trajectories in real time. A state-of-the-art, high-resolution imaging system captured and analyzed the complex airflow patterns in the free atmosphere, revealing intricate vortex patterns that significantly impact snowflake movement. Additionally, the study employed a high-precision optical sensor to track snowflake trajectories in the free atmosphere, revealing new insights into snow's anomalous transport behavior. By correlating the imaging data with snow's deposition patterns, we gained a deeper understanding of how the atmosphere's flow patterns influence snow's final destination, ultimately leading to the development of a predictive model based on the similarity principle.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is limited due to the complex mathematical optimizations required to update mental frameworks. To overcome these challenges, we suggest incorporating a novel technique from computer science, called distributed message passing, into a related theory called sparse occupational inference. By modifying this theory to accommodate changing environments, we develop a new framework that enables more efficient mental framework updates, ultimately leading to better performance. We test this framework in a simulated scenario, observing improved results with the same computational resources.

In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology, the task of processing large amounts of data in real-time is proving to be a substantial hurdle. As an alternative to standard compression methods, the use of machine learning algorithms has gained attention for real-time data reduction. Yet, data sets generated from scientific endeavors often comprise vast 3D data volumes characterized by significant portions of zeroes, non-uniform distribution of values, and high generation rates. Consequently, direct applications of popular compression methods along with standard compression methods yield unsatisfactory results. Therefore, to overcome these complications, the concept of Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE) is developed to tackle the challenges posed by these unique data characteristics. BCAE is implemented using Universal Neural Network and is studied in relation to its interpretability, adapting it to accommodate data by modifying its loss function according to data's non-uniform distribution and incorporating Stride parameters to address data's 3D structure. A thorough investigation of BCAE is conducted, including an examination of its ability to restore data of various dimensions, a study of how its reconstruction error varies with different data distributions, and an analysis of how adjusting its loss function and stride parameters affect the outcome. Additionally, an investigation is conducted on how BCAE's performance changes when data's sparsity is artificially manipulated, and finally, an investigation is conducted on how BCAE can be employed for real-time data reduction.

Utilizing Finzi's gravity theory that enhances interactions at large scales, we analyze galaxy clusters from a thermodynamic perspective, establishing a statistical model to derive thermodynamic equations and comparing clustering behavior with standard Newtonian gravity. We also explore the general distribution function's behavior as the clustering parameter varies in strength, with the finding that it differs from the standard Newtonian scenario.

A type of convex geometric hypergraph, known as cgh, comprises a set of subsets originating from strictly convex point sets in the plane. In this study, researchers explore a specific type of problem associated with cghs: saturation problems that correspond to earlier studied extremal issues. Using a mathematical approach, the study determines the maximum capacity of certain geometrically separated groups of points and establishes an exact value for a specific instance, as well as approximate values for seven out of eight possible geometric hypergraph configurations up to a specific level of accuracy, and a related but less accurate figure for the eighth configuration.

To gain a better understanding of the relative contributions of different processes, the angular distributions and energy spectra of $\alpha$ and deuterons resulting from breakup, transfer, and incomplete fusion have been measured and calculated. Cross-sections for the $^6$Li + $^{51}$V system were experimentally measured at energies near the Coulomb barrier, with theoretical estimates obtained through calculations with the finite range coupled reaction method using the \textsc{FRESCO} code. Calculations indicated that the cross-sections from various reaction channels including non-capture breakup and 1 proton, 1 neutron, and 1 deuteron transfer, compound nuclear decay, and incomplete fusion channels can effectively reproduce both the direct $\alpha$ production cross-sections and their angular distributions. Furthermore, the observed direct $\alpha$ production cross-sections align with other target systems, with higher $\alpha$ production compared to deuteron production observed. Analyzing the energy spectra of $\alpha$ and deuterons showed that the primary contributing channels are compound nuclear decay and transfer reactions, with the former exhibiting a broad distribution of angles and the latter displaying a strong anisotropy classifying the deuterons as being partially directed.

A previously overlooked ability in bio-inspired snake robots is dynamic vertical climbing. A novel locomotion technique mimicking the Pacific Lamprey's movement has been discovered, which enables a robot to navigate on flat surfaces while climbing at near-vertical inclines. A simplified model has been created to analyze the correlation between robot motion and actuation, resulting in the development of a new, adaptable robot inspired by the Pacific Lamprey. The new robot, called Trident, successfully demonstrates dynamic vertical climbing at speeds of up to 4.8 cm/s and can be easily fabricated using soft robotics technologies. Furthermore, its climbing mechanism allows it to move at speeds of up to 14.7 cm/s on inclined planes at a 45-degree angle.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework.

Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends on balancing device scheduling, transmission power, and frequency allocation to maximize overall system performance. In this study, we develop an innovative scheduling approach that integrates these elements by allocating frequencies and determining transmission power levels based on a two-stage optimization strategy combined with a bulging algorithm. This approach allows a base station to efficiently schedule communications and adjust parameters in real-time to reflect changing network conditions, such as varying D2D link distances. We validate our method through simulations and show that it significantly outperforms conventional scheduling techniques.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [25] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic, compressible flow with smooth solutions. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to this system in a specific mathematical space ensure the conservation of helicity. Additionally, similar results were found for both homogeneous incompressible Euler equations and the surface quasi-geostrophic equation.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations, focusing particularly on the large spectral parameter $k$ in a specified reference \cite{KlSjSt20}. They now examined how this work can be applied to the reflection coefficient and derived new asymptotic formulas for specific domains with potential functions and smooth, strictly convex boundaries.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of merging compact binary systems,
including higher-order effects of gravitational wave radiation, reveal that late-time
eccentricities of inspiraling binaries are typically underestimated by standard
models by up to 30 percent for heavy systems like 300-solar-mass binaries at
10 Hz, and less so for lighter binaries. By incorporating more refined equations,
a novel, accurate analytic formula for eccentricities at late times is formulated.
Furthermore, this model's results remain largely insensitive to the masses of the
binary components, with deviations below two percent, and generalizes previous
work by Peters and Mathews.

A proposed innovation combines the benefits of X-ray free-electron laser oscillators (XFELOs) and the undulator taper technique to create a groundbreaking X-ray laser. This is made possible by using an XFELO to seed a free-electron laser (FEL) amplifier with a specially tailored electron beam. The unique characteristics of the beam allow for the tail to be within the gain bandwidth of XFELO, generating a lasing seed that's used for further amplification. The remainder of the beam, outside gain bandwidth, can still be utilized in the FEL amplifier to produce a highly intense X-ray pulse. The experiment showed that this approach can achieve a higher average power and greater stability compared to a typical XFELO, while also offering the potential for higher peak powers and higher repetition rates in the future.

Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems.  Graph-based machine learning has made notable advancements lately, but detecting events in evolving networks still poses difficulties for current frameworks. Real-life occurrences typically involve sudden changes in network behavior patterns. Current methods for dynamic node representations are ineffective at capturing event-driven network changes.  To address these limitations, we propose a new approach, called DyGED, for recognizing events in evolving networks using a combination of temporal self-attention and structural awareness.  Through extensive testing on diverse datasets, we demonstrate that DyGED consistently outperforms alternative methods in accuracy, achieving up to an 8.5% improvement.  Notably, it also offers improved robustness and scalability compared to existing solutions.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show how these theoretical solutions can be accurately reproduced in Lagrangian hydrodynamic simulations, thereby validating and verifying these codes for a range of scenarios.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples, and, to enhance accuracy, recent deep learning methods have been developed for histopathological analysis. These studies used data collected from institutions in North America and Europe, and our research presents an updated model that integrates data from the CAD1065 CRC challenge. Our study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of deep learning models in characterizing polyps with varying sizes and shapes, and, to address data imbalance issues, we employed two techniques - re-sampling and re-labelling. Our models were trained and tested in ten rounds, and our key findings include the improvement of F1-score by 5% through re-sampling, and the enhancement of macro F1-score by 13% through re-labelling. When applied to unseen data, our models demonstrated a macro F1-score of 0.671 for classification, and a 0.942 area under the ROC curve for ranking.

In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish a comprehensive single-letter representation of the optimal normalized leakage in this adversarial scenario, along with a stochastic coding method that reaches this optimum. Interestingly, our analysis shows that both the sender and receiver are entirely unaware of the source distribution. We also explore extensions to the original problem where the adversary is allowed to make multiple guesses. In particular, we investigate cases where the adversary is restricted to outputting a single symbol or a finite set of symbols, with our analysis generalized to the case of distributed source coding.

Deep learning-trained generative models can function as a prior in under-determined inverse problems such as generating images from limited measurements, like a sparse dataset. A new hierarchical generative model called MrSARP is introduced in this research, specifically designed for Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) image generation. The MrSARP model consists of two components: the image-level generative network and the scene-level geometric regression network that maintains the position of targets and their characteristics. The effectiveness of the MrSARP model was tested on a simulated dataset, producing high-quality images and accurately preserving the location and characteristics of targets.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, typically to a single time.  The framework functions seamlessly with standard quantum computers generating random states, even without quantum gates.  We showcase the methodology's utility in an experimental simulation using a random instance of the exact 3-AT problem and an approximate variant of the Bin Packing Problem.

A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The Gaussian-Hermite division algorithm is used to find the intersection points, and a generalized formula is used to calculate the overlap area of the sectors formed by the secant lines and the ellipses. The area of the overlapping polygon is then calculated by summing the segment areas of the secant lines and the ellipses, and subtracting the segment areas of the overlapping secant lines and the ellipses. The segment area is calculated using a formula that depends on the coordinates of the ellipse vertices and the secant line intercepts.

Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time counterpart of Q-learning under the entropy-regularized exploratory process framework. To handle the collapse of the traditional Q-function in continuous time, we derive a first-order approximation and establish its solvability in a closed-form manner for specific initial conditions. Furthermore, we analyze the q-function's rate of convergence and explore its connection to the instantaneous advantage rate function.

Quantum magnets with coplanar spin exchange exhibit intricate magnetic dynamics. On the triangular lattice Hubbard model, researchers discover magnetic excitations with a unique pattern of wavevectors and polaron-like characteristics, influencing the model's phase transitions and behavior. However, magnetic excitations of this type are theoretically possible only if certain symmetry constraints are met, which is not the case for this model at half-filling. Further investigation reveals that these constraints are satisfied at low temperatures, allowing for the stabilization of these excitations through symmetry-breaking phase shifts, but only at points where the excitations would otherwise vanish. Introducing a small triangular-lattice dimerization drives these excitations to the edges of the magnetic Brillouin zone, creating a continuous spectrum that extends to all wavevectors at critical intensity. A theoretical framework that accounts for spin exchange and orbital correlation is consistent with experimental results and provides a comprehensive understanding of magnetic excitations, suggesting that early experiments may have overlooked these modes.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and robust two-stage approach that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine. Firstly, a specialized search window is dynamically generated for each vertebra based on the position of the preceding one and the intensity profile of the vertebral bodies, helping to narrow down the possible locations of new vertebrae. Following this step, an optimized registration method is used to accurately calculate the position of each vertebra. To evaluate the performance of this approach, three publicly accessible datasets with a total of 310 CT scans were used, as well as a dataset of 54 MRI scans. The results show that this method achieves average localization errors of 3.46 vertebral bodies and 2.69 discs, with an overall accuracy rate of 91.96% for vertebrae and 92.78% for discs on the CT scans. A significant improvement in accuracy can be observed compared to the state-of-the-art methods, particularly in cases of severe pathologies. The results for the MRI scans reveal a relatively lower accuracy rate, primarily due to the inherent limitations of low-resolution MRI images.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The use of natural sciences-inspired statistics, like the Gibbs-Boltzmann distribution, enables calculations of state transition probabilities, currently primarily applied in theoretical discussions. Despite this, the connection between probability theory and thermodynamics remains underexplored. The present work aims to establish the fundamental link between the probability theory's cumulant-generating functions and thermodynamics, independent of specific probability measures. It is demonstrated that gauge invariance is achieved when using the relative entropy as the thermodynamic average. The derived scaled cumulant-generating functions consistently describe time evolutions of thermodynamic quantities, like entropy production and entropy change. The study showcases the broad applicability of these functions in stochastic thermodynamics, particularly in addressing entropy's meaning and sign. The proposed approach is expected to stimulate a fresh, probabilistic perspective on the intersection of probability theory and thermodynamics.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

This study explores the transmission of energy between two closely positioned piezoelectric materials, focusing on the lateral force impact, electrical coupling, and distance between them. It outlines the setup and examines its eigenvalues and eigenfunctions in detail. Then, research findings on energy transfer through lateral force, electrical coupling, and gap distance are presented and discussed.

We explore a cutting-edge technique for optically manipulating polariton condensates at a microscale, taking into account real-world imperfections in laser beam precision. By prioritizing a broader excitation coverage over spectral coherence, we develop a simplified approach for generating micro-scale polariton condensates, utilizing non-resonant excitation energy profiles. Our method leverages a linear antenna-like system and a coherent feedback mechanism which enhances emission stability and strengthens the macroscopic occupation of the research team. Despite potential distortions in antenna resonance, we show that the emitted light remains strongly coupled, exhibiting a single, unified emission spectrum. Our approach offers a feasible and efficient solution for producing robust polariton condensates, even when dealing with excitation field irregularities.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris still unknown. Analyzing grain size and sublimation rate is essential in comprehending the environment that contributes to planetary disintegration. In this study, simulations of gas and particle mixtures surrounding K2-22b were conducted to develop a debris cloud formation model. Models were run under different thermal setups, with and without taking particle collisions into account. Balancing evaporation and sublimation led to the development of a debris cloud composed of small particles (<1 micrometers), and the results align with observed transit data. Particle collisions against the disk's inner boundary were found to significantly impact cloud morphology, suggesting that a large radius is achieved only through mass addition from collisions. In particular, collisions in the early stages of the disk can explain the observed transit patterns, and a subsequent growth of particles can be limited by thermal factors or the disk's overall mass.

We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a condition that guarantees its existence and is easy to verify. This leads to a simple method for calculating the virtual cohomology of the Milnor fiber, which we call the Milnor class. Our approach is flexible and allows for adaptation to various function field scenarios, as well as a presentation of the class in a specific, simplified format. Additionally, we derive corollaries that provide insight into the monodromy group and provide a formula for calculating the signature of the Milnor fiber.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this tool facilitates data preparation, feature engineering, and other data transformation operations. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple VS projects that can be easily installed as a NuGet package. At its core, Daany utilizes the DataFrame data structure, complemented by data science and linear algebra capabilities, including time series decomposition (SSA, STL, ARIMA) and optimization methods (SGD). The library also integrates matrix and vector operations, as well as data plotting functionality. Daany's implementation bears similarities to Python's Pandas library. This guide serves as a comprehensive developer manual, outlining Daany's features, functionality, and usage, as well as a listing of related papers.

I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic physical principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical terms, as he was more comfortable doing so.

We investigate the space charge in a plasma filled tube under conditions of non-equilibrium using the Fokker-Planck-Fokker-Landau collision model. By assuming the plasma distribution function has two components, our study derives the electron distribution function through Fourier transform, with results displayed in momentum space. We analyze the coherence effects, imaginary part, and total energy, in relation to the De Broglie wavelength. Furthermore, we demonstrate how generalized thermodynamic properties can facilitate the calculation of ionization rates in astrophysical contexts.

The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation. The subsequent reconnection process and subsequent island formation lead to the formation of a second magnetic flux rope, or second island, within the initial reconnection site. However, in our specific scenario, this second island formed on the opposite side of the initial one, rather than between them.

This document provides a summary of the content from a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer.  Throughout the course, we explore the technical foundations of these intelligent assistants, drawing from fields such as natural language processing, graphical models, deep learning, and reinforcement learning.  We then use this knowledge to create a realistic computer simulation of the assistant's training and learning, as well as its interactions with the expert software engineer.  We examine how this intelligent system can address various complexities in solving tasks, processing information, navigating the digital world, and understanding and generating human language.
